title: Iowa Department of Revenue — PARKING, INC DBA KECK PARKING (DO) 2026
text:
PARKING, INC. DBA KECK PARKING (DO) 2026
BEFORE THE IOWA DEPARTMENT OF REVENUE
HOOVER STATE OFFICE BUILDING
DES MOINES, IOWA
IN THE MATTER OF
PARKING, INC. DBA KECK PARKING DECLARATORY ORDER
475 SW 5TH ST
DES MOINES IA 50309-4666
DOCKET NO. 1213390
SALES/USE/EXCISE TAX
Pursuant to a Petition for Declaratory Order (“Petition”) filed with the Iowa Department of
Revenue (“Department”) by Parking, Inc. DBA Keck Parking (“Petitioner”) on January 22, 2026, and in
accordance with Iowa Code section 17A.9 (2026) and Iowa Administrative Code rule 701—4.7(17A),
“Declaratory order-in general,” the Director issues the following order.
I. FACTS
The facts below are based on the Petition, a response to a request for information provided by
Petitioner on February 26, 2026, and a Management Agreement (“Agreement”) between Petitioner and
Federal Home Loan Bank of Des Moines (“FHLB”).
Petitioner is a company that is retained by the owners of parking facilities to manage and operate
those parking facilities. Petitioner has entered into a contract with FHLB to manage and operate a parking
facility owned by FHLB. The parking facility contains spaces that FHLB plans to use for its own purposes
and additional parking spaces that will be offered for a fee to individuals and businesses for daily or
monthly parking. Petitioner describes FHLB as a federally chartered entity.
Petitioner provided a copy of the Agreement and describes the way in which it manages and
operates the parking facility. Under the Agreement, Petitioner is to act as FHLB’s agent and is responsible
for the operation and maintenance of the parking facility. These responsibilities include opening an
operating account with seed money from FHLB. Per the Agreement, funds from this account are to be

used for the operating costs of the parking facility. The Agreement also requires that Petitioner collect
parking fees from customers and place them into the operating account. Petitioner states that it will
follow this procedure if it is deemed to be acting as an agent for FHLB. If Petitioner is deemed the seller,
then the Petition states that Petitioner would deposit these amounts into its own account. This order will
evaluate Petitioner’s sales tax liability under the provided Agreement that Petitioner states it has entered
into.
Petitioner receives a management fee for its services for which it issues itself a check from the
operating account. The funds from the operating account are not to be commingled with any of
Petitioner’s other funds. The Agreement also requires that Petitioner write checks from the operating
account for the operation of the parking facility, provide reports on expenditures to FHLB, and serve
various customer service, maintenance, and advertising functions.
II. ISSUES PRESENTED
Petitioner presented the following questions for consideration:
1. Whether Petitioner must collect and remit sales tax on the sales price of the parking spaces
in the parking garage owned by FHLB.1
2. Whether this determination changes based on whether Petitioner acts as an agent of FHLB.
III. STANDARD OF REVIEW
Declaratory Orders under the Iowa Administrative Procedure Act:
Iowa Code chapter 17A, the Iowa Administrative Procedure Act (“IAPA”), was enacted “to provide
a minimum procedural code for the operation of all state agencies when they take action affecting the
rights and duties of the public.” Iowa Code § 17A.1(2). Under the IAPA, “[a]ny person may petition an
1 In the Petition, Petitioner asked whether the sales price of the parking spaces is subject to Iowa sales tax and
asked whether it “must collect and remit sales tax on these transactions.” In its response to a request for
additional information, it asked whether it “should” collect and remit sales tax on these amounts. This order will
address Petitioner’s obligation to collect and remit sales tax.
2

agency for a declaratory order as to the applicability to specified circumstances of a statute, rule, or order
within the primary jurisdiction of the agency.” Id. § 17A.9(1)(a). The IAPA also describes agency rights and
responsibilities with respect to declaratory order proceedings. Id. § 17A.9(8). Pursuant to Iowa Code
section 17A.9(2), the Department adopted Iowa Administrative Code rule 701—4.7, which outlines
department-specific rules governing declaratory orders.
The purpose of a declaratory order is to provide a “generally available means for persons to obtain
reliable information about agency administered law as it applies to their particular circumstances.” Sierra
Club Iowa Chapter v. Iowa Dep’t of Transp., 832 N.W.2d 636, 647 (2013) (citing Arthur Earl Bonfield,
Amendments to Iowa Administrative Procedure Act, Report on Selected Provisions to Iowa State Bar
Association and Iowa State Government, 1–8 (1998)). Declaratory orders are not contested cases that
“entitle parties affected by the agency action to an adversarial hearing” in order to “adjudicate disputed
facts pertaining to particular individuals in specific circumstances.” Greenwood Manor v. Iowa Dep’t of
Pub. Health, State Health Facilities Council, 641 N.W.2d 823, 834 (Iowa 2002); see also Iowa Code §
17A.12. Instead, the IAPA “contemplates declaratory rulings by administrative agencies on purely
hypothetical sets of facts.” City of Des Moines v. Pub. Emp’t Relations Bd., 275 N.W.2d 753, 758 (Iowa
1979).
As such, “[t]he procedure established by section 17A.9 allows persons to seek formal opinions on
the effect of future transactions and arrange their affairs accordingly.” Bennett v. Iowa Dep’t of Nat. Res.,
573 N.W.2d 25, 26 (Iowa 1997). Declaratory orders issued by an administrative agency do, however, have
“the same status and binding effect as any final order issued in a contested case proceeding.” Iowa Code
§ 17A.9(7). The Department’s rules governing declaratory orders are consistent with this understanding
of the role of declaratory orders in administrative procedure. See Iowa Admin. Code r. 701—4.7.
3

IV. DISCUSSION
A. The service at issue is subject to sales tax in Iowa
Petitioner requests a decision on its obligation to collect and remit sales tax on the parking spaces
offered to customers in the garage owned by FHLB. We begin by evaluating whether the service at issue
is a taxable service. Iowa imposes sales tax on “the sales price from the furnishing of services as defined
in section 423.1.” Iowa Code § 423.2(5). Further, the “sales price of any of the . . . enumerated services
[listed in subsection 423.2(6)] is subject to the tax imposed by subsection 5.” Id. § 423.2(6). Included in
the list of taxable services enumerated by the Code is “[p]arking facilities.” Id. § 423.2(6)(ak). This section
is implemented by Iowa Administrative Code rule 701—211.12. Iowa Administrative Code rule 701—
211.12(1) states, “[p]ersons engaged in the business of operating a parking facility for a fee are selling a
service subject to sales tax.” Under Iowa Administrative Code rule 701—211.12(2), a parking facility is
“any place that is used for parking a vehicle for consideration.” This subrule goes on to state, “[I]t is
irrelevant whether the charge is by the hour, day, month, or any other period of time.”
Petitioner provides an Agreement it has in place with FHLB to operate a parking garage owned by
FHLB, selling parking spaces to individuals and to area businesses for various periods of time. These
customers pay for the use of these spaces. Therefore, the space in question is being used to park vehicles
for consideration as described by Iowa Administrative Code rule 701—211.12(1). Therefore, the space in
question is a parking facility. The described service is the operation of a parking facility where, under the
Agreement with FHLB, Petitioner performs tasks for the daily operation of a parking facility. The service
at issue is subject to sales tax in Iowa, subject to any potential exemptions.
B. The exemptions raised in the Petition do not apply to Petitioner
In the Petition and in Petitioner’s additional response to a request for information, Petitioner
discusses exemptions relevant to federal entities. Specifically, Petitioner discusses the exemption in Iowa
Code section 423.3(31)(a), which exempts from sales tax the sales price of tangible personal property sold
4

to and services furnished to “a tax-certifying or tax-levying body of the state or a governmental subdivision
of the state, including . . . all divisions, boards, commissions, agencies, or instrumentalities of state,
federal, county, municipal, or tribal government.” In its response to a request for information, Petitioner
also referenced an argument about the constitutionality of a state taxing the federal government, but did
not further evaluate the potential applicability of such an argument.
Petitioner is not a federal entity and has not provided any information on making sales to a federal
entity. Petitioner asserts that FHLB is a federal entity and discusses these exemptions as being relevant to
FHLB. Iowa Code section 17A.9(1)(b)(2) prohibits the Department from issuing a declaratory order " . . .
that would substantially prejudice the rights of a person who would be a necessary party and who does
not consent in writing to the determination of the matter by a declaratory order proceeding." Because
FHLB is not a party to the Petition and has not consented to be bound by this order, the order will not
evaluate exemptions as they may apply to FHLB or FHLB’s sales tax liability.
C. Petitioner is not a seller who is a retailer
According to Iowa Code section 423.14(1)(a), sales tax “shall be collected by sellers who are
retailers or by their agents.” Iowa Code section 423.1(53) defines “seller” as “any person making sales,
leases, or rentals of personal property or services.” Iowa Code section 423.1(47) defines “retailer” as
“every person engaged in the business of selling tangible personal property, specified digital products, or
taxable services at retail . . . from which revenues are derived.”
According to the Petition and the Agreement, Petitioner is tasked with providing customer
service, collecting customer payments, advertising the parking garage, maintaining the parking garage,
and other operational tasks. According to the provided Agreement, Petitioner does not retain the revenue
from these sales. Rather, Petitioner places these amounts into an operating account for FHLB. Petitioner
is paid a flat fee by FHLB out of the operating account for its services. Although Petitioner is soliciting
customers and taking payments in exchange for parking, it does not own the parking spaces that are being
5

offered for a fee and it is not deriving revenues from these sales. Rather, Petitioner is a service provider
that collects payments and places them into the operating account as mandated by the Agreement.
Therefore, Petitioner is not obligated to collect and remit Iowa sales tax as a “seller who is a retailer”
under Iowa Code section 423.14(1)(a).
D. Petitioner is obligated to collect and remit sales tax in its capacity as an agent
The service of “parking facilities” is subject to sales tax under Iowa Code section 423.2(6)(ak). As
discussed above, Petitioner is not a “seller who is a retailer.” Under Iowa Code section 423.14(1)(a), sales
tax “shall be collected by sellers who are retailers or by their agents.” Petitioner asks about its obligation
to collect and remit sales tax as FHLB’s agent. An agency relationship requires “(1) manifestation of
consent by one person, the principal, that another, the agent, shall act on the former's behalf and subject
to the former's control and (2) consent by the latter to so act. Vroegh v. Iowa Dep’t of Corr., 972 N.W.2d
686, 707 (Iowa 2022) (quoting Pillsbury Co. v. Ward, 250 N.W.2d 35, 38 (Iowa 1977)). The Agreement
states in Article IX Paragraph C, “[Petitioner] shall be deemed [FHLB’s] agent for performance of the
operation and maintenance responsibilities assumed by [Petitioner] under this Agreement.” The inclusion
of this clause indicates mutual consent by Petitioner and FHLB for Petitioner to act as an agent.
In addition to the Agreement specifically stating that Petitioner is acting as an agent in the
operation of the parking garage, the Agreement as a whole and the facts provided in the Petition indicate
that Petitioner is acting as an agent. Article III section A of the Agreement lists requirements of Petitioner.
This section requires Petitioner to manage all contracts related to the parking operation on FHLB’s behalf.
This clause also requires that Petitioner provide copies of service contracts to FHLB upon request, which
also indicates that Petitioner is primarily in charge of these contractual relationships. This section also
requires Petitioner to set up an operating account on FHLB’s behalf with funds supplied by FHLB and
requires Petitioner to use the funds to operate the parking facility and place all revenues in the fund. The
requirements that Petitioner manage these contracts and operate the parking facility in this manner
6

indicate that Petitioner is acting on FHLB’s behalf under its control in the operation of the parking facility
and that both Petitioner and FHLB have agreed to this arrangement in the Agreement. Petitioner is not a
“seller who is a retailer” under Iowa Code section 423.14(1)(a) as discussed above, but operating a parking
facility is a service that is subject to sales tax. Because Petitioner is acting as an agent in the sale of the
taxable service at issue, it is obligated to collect and remit sales tax only in its capacity as an agent of FHLB
under the provided Agreement and facts.
V. CONCLUSION
Operating a parking facility is a service that is subject to Iowa sales tax under Iowa Code section
423.2(6)(ak). For purposes of FHLB’s parking facility, Petitioner is not a “seller who is a retailer” under
Iowa Code section 423.14(1)(a). However, Petitioner is obligated to collect and remit Iowa sales tax only
in its capacity as an agent of FHLB under the provided Agreement and facts. If FHLB is not required to
collect sales tax for furnishing the service of parking facilities, Petitioner is also not required to collect
sales tax in its role as FHLB’s agent; however, the Director cannot evaluate whether FHLB is required to
collect sales tax in this declaratory order.
ORDER
THEREFORE, based on the facts presented, foregoing reasoning, and applicable provisions of the
law, the questions presented in Petitioner’s Petition for Declaratory Order, Docket No. 1213390 are
answered above.

By ______________________________
Mary Mosiman, Director

NOW, on this 12th day of December 2008, this matter comes before the Administrator of the
Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division on the Order to Review the Proposed Decision.
I. STATEMENT OF REVIEW.
The record in this docket discloses that on February 1, 2008, the Iowa Department of Public
Safety (DPS) filed an administrative hearing complaint against Bowman Ventures, Inc. (Licensee). The
complaint alleged that on February 2, 2007, the Licensee or an agent or employee of the Licensee sold
or supplied an alcoholic beverage to a person under the legal age, in violation of Iowa Code §
123.49(2)(h). The complaint further alleged that the February 2, 2008, violation was the Licensee’s
second violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) within a period of two years.1
A Notice of Hearing scheduled the matter for a hearing on March 7, 2008. The Licensee
requested and was granted continuance of the matter to April 1, 2008. On that date, a hearing was
1 On October 27, 2006, the Licensee’s employee, Cole Eugene Bultman, was criminally charged and convicted of a
sale-to-minor violation under Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). On February 1, 2007, the Division imposed a $500.00 civil
penalty against the Licensee’s license for a first violation of the section.

held before an administrative law judge (ALJ) in accordance with Iowa Code Chapters 17A and 123.
Assistant Attorney General John Lundquist represented the DPS. The Licensee was represented by
Tammy Bowman (Bowman). Bowman is the sole owner of the Licensee.
On April 22, 2008, the ALJ issued a Proposed Decision which imposed a $1,500 civil penalty against
the Licensee’s license and suspended the license for a period of 30 days. The Licensee’s timely request
for review of the Proposed Decision followed.
On May 27, 2008, the Administrator issued an Order granting the Licensee’s request for
review. The parties were given the opportunity to file exceptions and present briefs in support of their
respective positions. The exceptions and brief of the appealing party were due no later than the close
of business on June 20, 2008. Responsive briefs were due no later than the close of business on July
21, 2008. No exceptions or briefs were filed in the matter.
Upon the motion of a party to the hearing or upon the Administrator’s own motion, the
Administrator may reverse or modify any finding of fact if a preponderance of the evidence will
support a determination to reverse or modify the finding. Iowa Code § 17A.15(3). Moreover, the
Administrator may reverse or modify any conclusion of law that the Administrator finds to be in error.
Id.
II. STATEMENT OF LAW.
The alcoholic beverages industry is highly regulated. Iowa Code Chapter 123 was enacted by
the Iowa Legislature “to protect the welfare, health, peace, morals and safety” of Iowans. Iowa Code §
123.1. All provisions of Chapter 123 are to be “liberally construed for the accomplishment of that
purpose.” Id. The trafficking of alcoholic beverages affects the public’s interest to the extent that it is
2

prohibited except as provided in Chapter 123. Id. It is unlawful to manufacture for sale, possess or
transport liquor, wine or beer except under the terms enumerated in Chapter 123. Iowa Code § 123.2.
“Legal age” is a defined term meaning “twenty-one years of age or more.” Iowa Code
§ 123.3(19). Selling or providing an alcoholic beverage to an underage person without exercising
“reasonable care to ascertain” whether the person is of the legal drinking age, is a violation of
Chapter 123. Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). A violation of Chapter 123 or the rules of the Division by an
employee or agent of the licensee is deemed an act of the licensee and subjects the licensee’s license to a
civil penalty, suspension or revocation. 185 IAC 4.8.
The administrative penalties for violations of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) are set by statute.
Under the statute, the first violation of the section “shall” subject a licensee’s license to a civil penalty in
the amount of $500.2 Iowa Code § 123.50(3)(a). A second violation within two years “shall” subject
the licensee’s license to a $1,500 civil penalty and a 30-day license suspension. Iowa Code §
123.50(3)(b). The statutory penalties become progressively more severe as the number of
sale-to-minor violations increase. A criminal conviction is not a prerequisite to the imposition of a civil
penalty or the suspension or revocation of a license. Iowa Code
§ 123.39(1)(c).
When a licensee establishes that reasonable inquiry was made to determine whether the
purchaser was of legal age, the licensee’s violation for selling the alcoholic beverage to the underage
person is legally excused. Iowa Code § 123.49(3).
III. STATEMENT OF THE ISSUES.

Did the Licensee’s employee violate Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) by selling an alcoholic beverage
to an underage person knowing or failing to exercise reasonable care to ascertain whether the person
was under the legal age?
May the Licensee avoid the $1,500 civil penalty and 30-day license suspension by asserting the
affirmative defense offered through a pilot project of the Division when the TIPS training completed
by the Licensee’s employees was sponsored by a former employee and not by the Division?
IV. STATEMENT OF THE FACTS.
In 2003, the Division obtained a grant from the Governor’s Traffic Safety Bureau to sponsor
“value-added” TIPS training for all on-premises licensees located in Iowa City. TIPS is a national
for-profit program designed to teach servers and sellers of alcoholic beverages how to prevent underage
sales, sales to intoxicated persons and drunk driving. The “value-added” portion of the program was
training about the ordinances and regulations unique to Iowa City and information about the
procedures used in alcohol compliance checks by Iowa City officers. The training was co-taught by
Division employees and Iowa City police officers, all of whom were certified TIPS trainers. Proposed
Decision, pages 2 and 3.
The “value-added” TIPS program was offered in Iowa City in 2003 and 2005, as a pilot project.
As part of the pilot project, the Division offered a limited affirmative defense to licensees if an employee
successfully completed the Division sponsored program, but subsequently sold an alcoholic beverage
to an underage person. Proposed Decision, page 3.
4

Information about the “value-added” TIPS training and affirmative defense was disseminated
to licensees through brochures. The 2003 brochure contained the following information about the
affirmative defense:
TIPS training offered by the Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division through the
pilot project may be used by a licensee for a limited period as an affirmative
defense against civil penalties for alcohol sales to minors. In order for a licensee
to use the defense, the employee cited must have been certified through the
program prior to the offense. The affirmative defense may be used once for
violations occurring after the training takes place and may not be applied to
pending violations. Employees cited for
alcohol sales to minors may not use training as an affirmative defense and will
be subject to the same criminal penalties as those not certified.
The 2005 brochure contained essentially the same information, but specified that use of the affirmative
defense was limited to the two-year period following completion of the program. Licensee’s Exhibits 7
and 8.
During the time that the Division was offering the “valued-added” TIPS program, other
groups were also offering TIPS training in Iowa City. The groups included licensees offering in-house
training and beer wholesalers. Although the training offered by the groups was part of the national
TIPS program, some of the programs were shorter and less thorough than the Division sponsored
program. Moreover, the training did not include the “valued-added” portion offered by the Iowa City
5

Police Department. Only the “value-added” TIPS training with information about Iowa City laws
qualified for the affirmative defense. Proposed Decision, page 4.
On May 23, 2005, Jodie Neuzil (Neuzil) successfully completed an in-house TIPS training
program which was offered by the Iowa City Moose Lodge where Neuzil was employed. After
completing the training, Neuzil received a TIPS certification card indicating Christine Garling as the
TIPS trainer. Garling was neither an employee of the Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division, nor the Iowa
City Police Department.
Sometime later, Neuzil was hired to work as a server in the Licensee’s establishment. During
the interview process, Bowman asked Neuzil if she had been TIPS trained. Neuzil responded that she
had successfully completed a TIPS training program that had been offered by her former employer.
Neuzil offered her TIPS training certification card to Bowman as proof of the training. Licensee’s
Exhibit “A.”
In August 2005, Bowman participated in the “value-added” TIPS training program sponsored
by the Division in conjunction with the Iowa City Police Department. After
successfully completing the training, Bowman received a TIPS training certification card similar to the
card issued to Neuzil. During the training, Bowman was told that the “value-added” training would
act like a “get-out-of-jail-free” card if an owner, employee or agent of the Licensee sold or served an
alcoholic beverage to an underage person. Bowman assumed that Neuzil’s TIPS training was the same
as hers and that the affirmative defense would apply if Neuzil sold or served an alcoholic beverage to an
underage person. Proposed Decision, pages 4 and 5.
6

On February 1, 2007 and February 2, 2007, Iowa City police officers conducted compliance
checks to determine whether establishments would sell or provide an alcoholic beverage to an underage
person. Prior to the compliance checks, the participating underage informants were required to empty
their pockets in the presence of an officer to ensure that they carried only their own valid Iowa driver’s
license and the money provided to them by officers to purchase the alcoholic beverages. Moreover, the
underage informants were instructed to answer truthfully if asked their age and to provide their own
valid Iowa driver’s license if asked for identification. Further, each informant was photographed as
evidence of their appearance on the night of the compliance checks. Proposed Decision, page 5.
On February 2, 2007, several undercover officers and an underage informant entered the
Licensee’s establishment to conduct a compliance check. The informant approached the bar and
ordered a Bud Light from bartender Neuzil. Neuzil got the beer and then asked the informant for
identification. The underage informant produced her own valid driver’s license which was vertically
oriented indicating that the informant was underage on the date of issuance. Moreover, a red band
with the words “under age 21 until 4-15-07,” appeared above the informant’s picture.
Neuzil looked at the license and then sold the beer to the underage informant. A criminal
citation for selling alcohol to an underage person in violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) was issued
to Neuzil that evening. Following a trial, Neuzil was found not guilty and the charge
against her was dismissed. Proposed Decision, pages 5 and 6. The hearing complaint filed by
the DPS followed on February 1, 2008.
V. ANALYSIS.
7

In the instant case, the ALJ found that the preponderance of the evidence established that
Neuzil, an employee of the Licensee, sold an alcoholic beverage to an underage informant on February
2, 2007. Further, the ALJ found that Neuzil either knew or failed to exercise reasonable care to
ascertain whether the underage informant was of the legal drinking age. Id.
The sale on February 2, 2007, occurred under controlled circumstances with officers and
witnesses present. The driver’s license of the underage informant on the night of the compliance check
was vertically oriented and the words “under 21 until 4.15.07,” appeared in a red banner above the
informant’s picture. In the Proposed Decision, the ALJ found that, based on the photograph taken of
the informant on the night of the compliance check and the informant’s appearance and demeanor at
the hearing, the appearance of the informant was consistent with her age.
The narrower issue in the case, therefore, is whether the in-house TIPS training completed by
Neuzil while working for the Moose Lodge qualifies for the affirmative defense granted under the
“value-added” TIPS training sponsored by the Division. Essentially, the Licensee argues that, because
Neuzil had a current TIPS training card at the time she made the sale to the underage informant, the
Licensee is entitled to assert the affirmative defense for the violation on February 2, 2007.
The Division’s offer, however, has always limited the affirmative defense to the Division sponsored
training that was held in conjunction with the Iowa City Police Department. The affirmative defense
was never intended to extend to any training than the Division’s “value-
added” TIPS training initiative. In that sense, the pilot project was very limited in its scope and
application, and the Division never intended to extend the incentive to all TIPS training.
8

Although Bowman concedes that Neuzil’s TIPS training was offered by her former employer,
Bowman essentially argues that the Licensee was misled by the Divison’s offer of a limited affirmative
defense for sale-to-minor violations under Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). The Administrator finds
Bowman’s argument to be without merit. The denial of the affirmative defense in the instant case is
consistent with the statements contained in the Divison’s brochures.
The underage informant had an appearance consistent with her age on the date of the
compliance check. When Neuzil asked the informant for identification, the informant produced her
own valid driver’s license. The license was vertically oriented and reflected the words, “under 21 until
4.15.07.” While Neuzil went through the motions of checking the identification, she either
miscalculated or failed to properly verify the informant’s age. Under no circumstances did Neuzil
exercise reasonable care to ascertain whether the informant was of legal drinking age.
The Administrator sees no legal reason to recognize an affirmative defense in the case.
Moreover, the Administrator believes that the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law and the
Decision and Order in the case should be affirmed.

carried only her valid driver’s license and had been
instructed to answer truthfully if asked her age. The

to accurately determine the customer’s age.

licensee’s first violation was based on a prohibited sale

through Iowa Code section 123.50(3)(b), has provided a
mandatory $1500 civil penalty and a 30 day license
suspension for a second violation of Iowa Code section
123.49(2)(h). The legislature has not provided any
exceptions to this statute nor has the Division promulgated
any rules establishing either an exception or an

NOW, on this 9th day of February 2011, this matter comes before the Administrator of the
Alcoholic Beverages Division (Division) on the Notice of Appeal filed by Codycal, Inc., d/b/a
Greenbriar Restaurant & Bar (Licensee).
Upon consideration of the information provided by the parties, the finding of fact, conclusion of
law and other information the administrator has affirmed the ALJ order dated October 12, 2010.
PROCEDURAL HISTORY
On April 12, 2010, the Iowa Department of Public Safety (DPS) filed an administrative hearing
complaint against the Licensee alleging that on or about August 25, 2009, an employee of the
Licensee sold or supplied an alcoholic beverage, wine or beer to a person under the legal age, in
violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h).
A hearing on the above captioned matter was held pursuant to the provisions of Iowa Code
chapters 17A and 123 on September 27, 2010. The hearing was held before presiding
administrative law judge (ALJ) Margaret LaMarche of the Department of Inspections and
Appeals. Attorney David Wetsch represented Codycal, Inc. (Licensee), and Assistant Attorney
General John Lundquist represented the DPS.
The ALJ issued a Proposed Decision on October 12, 2010 imposing a civil penalty of $500.00
for a first violation of selling or providing an alcoholic beverage to a patron under the legal age.
The Licensee timely filed a Notice of Appeal of the Proposed Decision to the Administrator of
the Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division.
In an Order dated October 27, 2010, the Administrator of the Division granted the Licensee’s
request for review and established a schedule for the parties to file objections or exceptions and
present briefs in support of their respective positions. The objections or exceptions and briefs of
the appealing party were due on November 29, 2010, and responsive briefs were due on or
before December 29, 2010. Let the record reflect that all briefs were timely filed by the parties.

PH 515.281.7400 FAX 515.281.7385 TOLL FREE 866.IowaABD WWW.IowaABD.com

BASIS FOR THE APPEAL
The Licensee’s objections and the basis for the appeal are based on that the ALJ erred in
imposing a $500.00 civil penalty for a first violation of Iowa Code
§ 123.49(2)(h). Specifically that the ALJ erred in concluding that the beverage sold or provided
to the underage person as an alcoholic beverage or a nonalcoholic beer and the ALJ erred in
placing the burden of proving compliance with the statute on the Licensee.
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. On August 25, 2009, Johnston Police Officers Tyler Tompkins and Rich Kirkeby conducted
alcohol compliance checks to determine whether liquor licensed establishments would sell an
alcoholic beverage to an underage person. The police department used two confidential
informants. CI #1 who was born on October 11, 1991, and was eighteen years old on August 25,
2009 and a CI #2 was born on May 23, 1990, and was nineteen years old.
2. CIs entered the Greenbriar Restaurant & Bar where as the following action took place. CI #2
ordered and paid for a bottle of Guinness beer without being asked for identification by the
Licensee’s employees. The transaction was witnessed firsthand by Officers Tompkins and
Kirkeby who were located in the same area.
3. In the ALJ Proposed Decision, the ALJ found that the preponderance of the evidence
established the Licensee’s employees sold and served a Guinness beer to CI #2 without
exercising reasonable care to ascertain whether the nineteen-year-old was of the legal drinking
age.
4. In the Proposed Decision, the ALJ acknowledged that the officers neither sampled nor tested
the liquid inside the bottle to verify it contained alcohol.
5. The Licensee does not dispute that Iowa Code § 17A.18(3) provides that “no revocation,
suspension, annulment, or withdrawal” may occur unless the Licensee is “given an opportunity
to show … compliance with all the lawful requirements for holding the license.” Section
17A.18(3) places the burden on the licensee when its license could be revoked, suspended,
annulled or withdrawn.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
It is a violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) to sell, give, or otherwise supply any alcoholic
beverage to a person, knowing or failing to exercise reasonable care to ascertain whether the
person is under legal age, or permit any person, knowing or failing to exercise reasonable care to
ascertain whether the person is under the legal age to consume any alcoholic beverage.
Iowa Code § 123.39(1) provides that the Administrator may suspend, revoke, or impose a civil
penalty against a liquor license for violation of any provision of Iowa Code chapter 123 and the
penalties for violations of § 123.49(2)(h) are set by statute. Pursuant to § 123.50(3)(a), the
mandatory penalty for a first sale-to-minor violation is a $500.00 civil penalty.
2

BASIS FOR DECISION
The Licensee seeks to avoid an administrative penalty by claiming that there is no evidence in
the record to support a finding that CI #2 was actually served an alcoholic beverage. The
Administrator has concluded based on the court records that the argument to be without merit.
The record in the case clearly shows that CI #2 ordered a Guinness while in the Licensee’s
establishment. The order was verified by the firsthand observations of Officers Tompkins and
Kirkeby, the statements of the CIs, and the cash register receipt detailing the sale. Moreover, the
Licensee’s employees made no claim that the bottle of Guinness contained a nonalcoholic beer
when they were confronted on the evening of the compliance check. Based on the evidence
presented, it is reasonable to conclude that the Licensee’s employees sold an alcoholic beverage
(beer) to CI #2 on the evening of August 25, 2009.
Moreover, the Licensee asserts that, because the Licensee’s license was not subject to revocation,
suspension, annulment, or withdrawal, the burden in the case of proof is on DPS. The Licensee’s
license was subject, at most, to a $500.00 civil penalty – not to revocation, suspension,
annulment, or withdrawal. By failing to address the contents of the Guinness bottle served to the
CI, DPS failed to carry the burden of proof. The Administrator observes that argument to also be
without merit. In a contested case hearing, the burden of going forward with the evidence to
establish a violation is on the State, but the burden of proving compliance with the statute shifts
to the licensee. McCrea v. Iowa Department of Transportation, 336 N.W.2d. 427 (Iowa 1983);
Iowa Code § 17A.18(3).
It is a violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) for a licensee or an employee of the Licensee to
sell, give, or otherwise supply liquor, wine or beer to any person knowing or failing to exercise
reasonable care to ascertain whether the person is under the legal age to consume alcoholic
beverages. The Iowa Supreme Court has recognized that at a minimum, the exercise of
reasonable care to ascertain the age of a person within the meaning of § 123.49(2)(h) requires the
licensee or employee to request identification from a person whose age is unknown and who
appears to be under the legal drinking age. Jim O., Inc. v. City of Cedar Rapids, 587 N.W.2d
476 478 (Iowa 1998). In the case at hand, ascertainment could have been easily overcome
simply by requiring CI #2 to furnish proof of age before serving the Guinness beer. Yet the
Licensee’s employees made no such effort.
The evidence in the case provides overwhelming support for the Administrator to conclude that
the Licensee’s employees sold, served or otherwise provided an alcoholic beverage to a person
under the legal age on August 25, 2009.
ORDER
Based on the information provided by the parties and the Code of Iowa, the Administrator hereby
ADOPTS the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, as well as the Decision and Order
proposed by the ALJ.

Greenbriar Restaurant & Bar, 5810 Merle Hay Road, Johnston, Iowa, shall pay a civil penalty of
$500.00 for the first violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2(h). The civil penalty is due and payable
to the “Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division,” 1918 SE Hulsizer Road, Ankeny, Iowa 50021, on
or before March, 11, 2011. Failure to timely pay the civil penalty shall result in further
administrative proceedings against liquor license number LC0020914.

agency action for the purpose of Iowa Code chapters 17A and 123. This Order becomes final,
unless a party to the hearing files a Petition for Judicial Review with the Iowa District Court
within 30 days from the date of the Order.
Moreover, the parties are notified that pursuant to Iowa Code § 17A.19(5), the filing of a petition
for judicial review does not automatically stay execution or enforcement of the Division’s action.
The Division may grant a stay on appropriate terms or other temporary remedies during the
pendency of judicial review. If the Division refuses to grant the stay or other temporary
remedies, the court may grant the relief.

reasonable care to ascertain the age of a person within the meaning of § 123.49(2)(h) requires the
licensee or employee to request identification from a person whose age is unknown and who
appears to be under the legal drinking age. Jim O., Inc. v. City of Cedar Rapids, 587 N.W.2d
476 478 (Iowa 1998). In the case at hand, ascertainment could have been easily overcome
simply by requiring CI #2 to furnish proof of age before serving the Guinness beer. Yet the
Licensee’s employees made no such effort.
3

The evidence in the case provides overwhelming support for the Administrator to conclude that
the Licensee’s employees sold, served or otherwise provided an alcoholic beverage to a person
under the legal age on August 25, 2009.
ORDER
Based on the information provided by the parties and the Code of Iowa, the Administrator hereby
ADOPTS the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law, as well as the Decision and Order
proposed by the ALJ.
IT IS ORDERED that liquor license number LC0020914, issued to Codycal, Inc., d/b/a
Greenbriar Restaurant & Bar, 5810 Merle Hay Road, Johnston, Iowa, shall pay a civil penalty of
$500.00 for the first violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2(h). The civil penalty is due and payable
to the “Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division,” 1918 SE Hulsizer Road, Ankeny, Iowa 50021, on
or before March, 11, 2011. Failure to timely pay the civil penalty shall result in further
administrative proceedings against liquor license number LC0020914.

On April 12, 2010, the Iowa Department of Public Safety (DPS) filed an
administrative hearing complaint against Codycal, Inc. d/b/a Greenbriar
Restaurant & Bar (licensee). The hearing complaint alleged that on or about
August 25, 2009, an employee of the licensee sold or supplied an alcoholic
beverage, wine, or beer to a person under the legal age, in violation of Iowa Code
section 123.49(2)(h). A hearing was held before Administrative Law Judge
Margaret LaMarche on September 27, 2010 at 8:30 a.m. at the office of the Iowa
Department of Inspections and Appeals Administrative Hearings Division,
Wallace State Office Building-Third Floor, Des Moines, Iowa. Assistant Attorney
General John Lundquist represented DPS. The licensee was represented by
attorney David Wetsch.
THE RECORD
The record includes the Hearing Complaint, Notice of Hearing, Appearance of
Counsel, Continuance Request and Continuance Orders, the testimony of
Johnston Police Officers Tyler Tompkins and Rich Kirkeby, and DPS Exhibits 1-6
(See Exhibit Index for description)
FINDINGS OF FACT
On August 25, 2009, the Johnston Police Department conducted an alcohol
compliance check to determine whether licensed liquor establishments in
Johnston would sell alcohol to an underage person. Two underage males agreed

DIA NO: 10DOCBL040
Page 2
to participate in the compliance check as confidential informants (CI). CI#1 was
born on October 11, 1991 and was 18 years old on August 25, 2009. CI#2 was
born on May 23, 1990 and was 19 years old. Officer Rich Kirkeby verified their
ages through Iowa Department of Transportation records. The confidential
informants turned over their wallets and other possessions and were only
permitted to carry their valid drivers’ licenses and a $20 bill to purchase
beverages. Office Kirkeby brought the drivers’ licenses of both confidential
informants to the hearing and showed them to the licensee’s attorney and to the
administrative law judge. The driver’s licenses were not submitted as exhibits.
Based on viewing the drivers’ license photographs, the confidential informants
had physical appearances that were generally consistent with their ages.
(Tompkins, Kirkeby testimony; DPS Exhibit 1)
Officer Kirkeby gave the confidential informants instructions for participating in
the undercover compliance check. The confidential informants were told to walk
into each establishment, order an alcoholic beverage, and to produce their
drivers’ licenses if asked for identification. If a sale was made they were told to
pay for the alcoholic beverage and walk out without touching it. Twenty-six
establishments were visited during the compliance check. Six of the twenty-six
establishments sold an alcoholic beverage to one or both informants.
Approximately one week later, both informants provided the Johnston police
department with written statements summarizing the sales. (Kirkeby testimony;
DPS Exhibits 3-4)
On August 26, 2009 at approximately 8:30 p.m., Officer Tompkins and Officer
Kirkeby entered the Greenbriar and sat in a booth that had a view of the bar area.
The confidential informants entered the Greenbriar after the officers and sat at a
table. Officer Tompkins could see the confidential informants from where he
was seated, and Officer Kirkeby turned around from time to time to view the
confidential informants. A waitress approached the confidential informants and
asked them what they wanted to drink. When they asked if there were any wine
specials, the waitress offered to bring them a wine menu. When the waitress
returned to take their order, CI#1 asked for a water, stating that he would
purchase a bottle of wine when the rest of their group arrived. CI #2 ordered a
“Guinness” beer in a bottle.
A second employee, later identified as Katie Cronin, served CI#2 the Guinness
and CI#1 his water. Neither the waitress nor Ms. Cronin asked CI#2 for
identification. Ms. Cronin provided CI#2 with an itemized bill for the

DIA NO: 10DOCBL040
Page 3
“Guinness,” which was $4.50 plus tax. The confidential informants paid with a
$20 bill, received change, and walked out of the restaurant. (Tompkins; Kirkeby
testimony; DPS Exhibits 1-4)
Officer Tompkins was in a position to see the entire transaction. He did not see
either employee involved with the sale ask CI#2 for identification. When the
officers walked past the table where the confidential informants had been sitting,
they saw the bottle of dark beer on the table. They did not sample or test the
liquid inside the bottle to verify that it contained alcohol. (Tompkins; Kirkeby
testimony)
Officer Kirkeby returned to the Greenbriar the following day to speak to the
manager. The manager identified employee Katie Cronin, whose name appeared
on the receipt given to CI#2, as the person who was working behind the beer and
the person who delivered the Guinness to CI#2. The manager told Officer
Kirkeby that the waitress, not Ms. Cronin, should be issued the citation for the
sale because it was the waitress’ job to check identification. However, Officer
Kirkeby decided to issue the criminal citation to Katie Cronin because she was
the one who delivered the beer to CI#2 and took the money for the beer. Katie
Cronin reported to the police station on August 27, 2009 and accepted a criminal
citation for serving alcohol to an underage person. Neither Greenbriar’s
manager nor Ms. Cronin told Officer Kirkeby that the Guinness served to the
confidential informant could have been non-alcoholic. The criminal citation was
later dismissed by the court for an unknown reason. (Tompkins; Kirkeby
testimony; DPS Exhibit 5)
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h)(2009) provides, in relevant part:
2. A person or club holding a liquor control license or retail
wine or beer permit under this chapter, and the person's or club's
agents or employees, shall not do any of the following:
...
h. Sell, give, or otherwise supply any alcoholic beverage, wine
or beer to any person, knowing or failing to exercise reasonable
care to ascertain whether the person is under legal age, or permit
any person, knowing or failing to exercise reasonable care to

DIA NO: 10DOCBL040
Page 4
ascertain whether the person is under legal age, to consume any
alcoholic beverage, wine, or beer.
The Iowa Code defines "legal age" as twenty-one years of age or more. Iowa
Code section 123.3(19)(2009).
185 IAC 4.8 states that the violation of the Act (Iowa Code chapter 123) by any
employee, agent, or servant of a licensee or permittee shall be deemed to be the
act of the licensee or permittee and shall subject the license to suspension or
revocation.
The burden of going forward with the evidence to establish a violation is on the
party filing the hearing complaint, but the alcoholic beverages division places the
burden of proving compliance with the statute on the licensee. See McCrea v.
Iowa Department of Transportation, 336 NW2d 427 (Iowa 1983); Iowa Code
section 17A.18(3)(2009).
The preponderance of the evidence established that on August 25, 2009, the
licensee’s employees sold and served a Guinness beer to an underage (19 year
old) confidential informant without exercising reasonable care to ascertain
whether the person was under the legal age. Neither the waitress nor the
employee who delivered the beer to the confidential informant asked him for
identification. At hearing, the licensee did not deny that one of its employees
sold and served CI#2 a “Guinness” for $4.50 on August 25, 2009 without first
requesting identification. The only defense offered by the licensee was the
assertion that the state failed to establish that the “Guinness” served to CI#2 was
an alcoholic beverage.
The state has gone forward with sufficient evidence to establish the illegal sale of
a bottle of Guinness beer to CI#2. The licensee offered no evidence to show that
Guinness makes a non-alcoholic beer or to show that the Greenbriar sells a non-
alcoholic Guinness beer. Officer Kirkeby spoke to the licensee’s manager on
August 26, 2009 and to Katie Cronin on August 27, 2009. Neither of them
claimed that the confidential informant had been served a non-alcoholic beer.
Based on this record, it is reasonable to conclude that the licensee’s employees
served and sold an alcoholic beverage (beer) to an underage confidential
informant, in violation of Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h)(2009).
Iowa Code section 123.50 provides, in relevant part:

DIA NO: 10DOCBL040
Page 5
123.50 Criminal and civil penalties.
...
3. If any licensee, wine permittee, beer permittee, or employee
of a licensee or permittee is convicted or found in violation of
section 123.49, subsection 2, paragraph "h", the administrator or
local authority shall, in addition to criminal penalties fixed for
violations by this section, assess a civil penalty as follows:
a. A first violation shall subject the licensee or permittee to a
civil penalty in the amount of five hundred dollars. Failure to
pay the civil penalty as ordered under section 123.39 shall result in
automatic suspension of the license or permit for a period of
fourteen days.
Pursuant to Iowa Code sections 123.50(3)(a), the mandatory administrative
sanction for a first offense sale to an underage person is a $500 civil penalty. A
criminal conviction is not a prerequisite to suspension, revocation or imposition
of a civil penalty. Iowa Code section 123.39(1)(c)(2009).
ORDER
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED, pursuant to Iowa Code sections 123.50(3)(a) and
123.39(4), that for a first offense sale to an underage person occurring on August
25, 2009, Codycal, Inc., d/b/a Greenbriar Restaurant & Bar, Liquor License No.
LC-20914, shall pay a civil penalty of five hundred dollars ($500) to the Alcoholic
Beverages Division within thirty (30) days of the issuance of this proposed
decision.

d/b/a David’s Place :

Liquor License No. LC0034106 : ADMINISTRATOR’S FINAL ORDER
______________________________________________________________________________
NOW, on this 17th day of December 2008, this matter comes before the Administrator of the
Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division on the Order to Review the Proposed Decision.
I. STATEMENT OF REVIEW.
The record in this docket discloses that on February 15, 2007, the Iowa Alcoholic Beverages
Division (Division) issued an Order to Dawit’s Restaurant, Inc. (Licensee) imposing a $500 civil penalty
for a first conviction of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h), by selling or providing an alcoholic beverage to a
person under the legal age. The violation, which occurred on March 3, 2006, is the Licensee’s first
violation within a two-year period.
The Licensee filed a Notice of Appeal requesting that the Order be reversed and that the civil
penalty be waived. A Notice of Hearing scheduled the matter for a hearing on April 9, 2007. The hearing
was subsequently rescheduled to January 11, 2008.
The record further discloses that on November 8, 2007, the Iowa Department of Public Safety
(DPS) filed an administrative hearing complaint with the Division alleging that on or about February 2,
2007, the Licensee or an employee or agent of the Licensee sold or supplied an alcoholic beverage to an

underage person in violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). The complaint further alleged that the
violation of February 2, 2007, was the second such violation within a period of two years. The matter was
scheduled for a hearing on January 11, 2008, as well.
On January 10, 2008, the matters were consolidated and rescheduled for a hearing on March 7, 2008. On
that date, an administrative hearing was held before an administrative law judge (ALJ) in accordance with
Iowa Code Chapters 17A and 123. Assistant Attorney General John Lundquist represented the Division
on the appeal and the DPS on the hearing complaint. The Licensee was represented by Attorney John
Beasley.
On March 26, 2008, the ALJ issued a Proposed Decision, which imposed a $500 civil penalty
against the Licensee’s license for the first violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) on March 3, 2006, and a
$1,500 civil penalty and a 30-day license suspension for the Licensee’s second violation of the section on
February 2, 2007.
On April 25, 2008, the Administrator issued an Order to Review the Proposed Decision on the
Administrator’s own motion to determine if the decision was consistent with agency precedent and
factually supported by the record. The parties were given the opportunity to file exceptions and present
briefs in support of their respective positions. The exceptions and briefs were due no later than the close
of business on May 26, 2008. No exceptions or briefs were filed in the matter.
Upon the motion of a party to the hearing or upon the Administrator’s own motion, the
Administrator may reverse or modify any finding of fact if a preponderance of the evidence will support a
determination to reverse or modify the finding. Iowa Code § 17A.15(3). Moreover, the Administrator
may reverse or modify any conclusion of law that the Administrator finds to be in error. Id.
II. STATEMENT OF LAW.

The alcoholic beverages industry is highly regulated. Iowa Code Chapter 123 was enacted by the
Iowa Legislature “to protect the welfare, health, peace, morals and safety” of Iowans. Iowa Code
§ 123.1. All provisions of Chapter 123 are to be “liberally construed for the accomplishment of that
purpose.” Id. The trafficking of alcoholic beverages affects the public’s interest to the extent that it is
prohibited except as provided in Chapter 123. Id. It is unlawful to manufacture for sale, possess or
transport liquor, wine or beer except under the terms enumerated in Chapter 123. Iowa Code § 123.2.
“Legal age” is a defined term meaning “twenty-one years of age or more.” Iowa Code
§ 123.3(19). Selling or providing an alcoholic beverage to an underage person, without exercising
“reasonable care to ascertain” whether the person is of the legal drinking age, is a violation of Chapter 123.
Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). A violation of Chapter 123 or the rules of the Division by an employee or
agent of the licensee is deemed an act of the licensee and subjects the licensee’s license to a civil penalty,
suspension or revocation. 185 IAC 4.8.
The administrative penalties for violations of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) are set by statute. Under
the statute, a first violation of the section “shall” subject a licensee’s license to a civil penalty in the amount
$500.1 Iowa Code § 123.50(3)(a). A second violation within two years “shall” subject the license to a
$1,500 civil penalty and a 30-day license suspension. Iowa Code § 123.50(3)(b). The penalties become
progressively more severe as the number of sale-to-minor violations increase. A criminal conviction is not
a prerequisite to the imposition of a civil penalty or the suspension or revocation of a license. Iowa Code §
123.39(1)(c).
1 When used in a statute, the word “shall” imposes a duty. Iowa Code § 4.1(30)(a).

When a licensee establishes that a reasonable inquiry was made to determine whether the
purchaser was of legal age, the licensee’s violation of selling the alcoholic beverage to the underage person
is legally excused. Iowa Code § 123.49(3).
III. STATEMENT OF THE ISSUES.
A. Did the Licensee satisfy all of the requirements to be eligible for the affirmative defense offered
through the Division sponsored TIPS training program?
B. May the Licensee avoid the $500 civil penalty mandated by Iowa Code § 123.50(3)(a) by
invoking the affirmative defense offered solely through a pilot project of the Iowa Alcoholic Beverages
Division, when the Licensee’s employee was criminally convicted under Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h)?
C. Should the Division be precluded or estopped from imposing an administrative sanction for the
Licensee’s first violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) because the Licensee relied on the Division’s public
announcement that a one-time affirmative defense would be available through the Division sponsored
TIPS training program if the employee making the sale was TIPS certified?
IV. STATEMENT OF THE FACTS.
On August 4, 2003, the undersigned Administrator issued a press release announcing a server
training program utilizing Training for Interventions Procedures (TIPS) for on-premises licensees located
in Johnson County. The TIPS program is designed to teach servers and sellers of alcoholic beverages how
to prevent underage sales or sales to intoxicated persons. The server training was offered free-of-charge to
licensees through a grant obtained from the Governor’s Traffic Safety Bureau. Proposed Decision, page 3.
The 2003 press release contained the following information about the affirmative defense:
Establishments participating in the TIPS training will be granted a one-time
affirmative defense, valid for a two-year period, whereby a business may avoid civil

prosecution if a sales-to-minor violation occurs in their establishment. In order
for the business to take advantage of the affirmative defense, the employee guilty
of the violation must have been TIPS certified at the time the violation occurred.
Though a business may avoid a civil penalty by asserting the affirmative defense,
the guilty employee will still be subject to a criminal fine.
Licensee’s Exhibit 3. [Emphasis Added].
The Division also circulated brochures promoting the four-hour Johnson County TIPS program.
The brochure stated that the TIPS program could be used by a licensee for a limited period as an
affirmative defense against civil penalties for alcohol sales to minors. The brochure further stated that
licensee or employee cited for selling or providing the alcoholic beverage to the minor could not use the
training as an affirmative defense to avoid the criminal penalties. Proposed Decision, pages 3 and 4.
The training sessions were held in Iowa City during a period commencing on August 4, 2003 and
ending on August 15, 2003. The sessions were taught by certified TIPS trainers from the Division and the
Iowa City Police Department. Certified TIPS trainers from the Sheraton Hotel in Iowa City also
participated in the training. Id.
Dawit Kidane (Kidane) is the manager and 25% shareholder of Dawit’s Restaurant, Inc. Kidane
managed Vito’s Bar and Grill in Iowa City for 15 years before opening David’s Place. Christopher
Lindsey (Lindsey) was an employee of Vito’s Bar and Grill during Kidane’s tenure as manager. When
Kidane opened David’s Place, Lindsey left Vito’s to work for Kidane at the new business. Proposed
Decision, page 4. Both Kidane and Lindsey successfully completed the Division sponsored TIPS program
while they were employed at Vito’s Bar and Grill. When Lindsey completed the course on August 8,

2003, a TIPS certification card was issued to him. The card was valid for three years.2 Licensee’s Exhibit
1.
On March 3, 2006, Lindsey was criminally cited for selling an alcoholic beverage to an underage
person in violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). Kidane, who was in the licensed establishment when the
citation was issued, informed the officers that Lindsay was TIPS trained. Kidane believed that by
notifying the officers of the TIPS training, the Licensee would receive the benefit of affirmative defense
offered under the Division’s TIPS training program.
On August 9, 2006, Lindsey voluntarily entered a plea of guilty to the violation without
informing the Licensee of his intention to do so. Lindsey’s guilty plea triggered a $500 civil penalty
against the Licensee’s license for the first violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) within two years. The
penalty was imposed in an Order issued by the Division on February 15, 2007. State’s Exhibit 1.
Kidane was surprised to receive the Order because he had informed officers that Lindsay had been TIPS
trained. Kidane consulted with an attorney, filed an appeal and obtained written confirmation of
Lindsey’s TIPS training. Proposed Decision, page 5.
On February 2, 2007, Iowa City police officers conducted compliance checks to determine whether
establishments would sell or provide an alcoholic beverage to an underage person. Prior to the compliance
checks, the participating informants were required to empty their pockets in the presence of an officer to
ensure that the informants carried only their own valid Iowa driver’s license and the money provided to
them by officers to purchase the alcoholic beverages. Moreover, the informants were instructed to answer
truthfully if asked their age and to provide their own valid Iowa driver’s license if asked for identification.
2 Although the TIPS training certificate was valid for three years, the affirmative defense was available to a licensee for two years
of completing the training program.

Further, each informant was photographed as evidence of their appearance on the night of the compliance
checks. Id.
Shortly after entering the Licensee’s establishment, the officers observed the Licensee’s bartender,
Alisha Hoversten (Hoversten), sell a beer to one of the underage informants without asking for
identification. Hoversten was criminally cited for violating Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). Although Kidane
was present in the establishment at the time of the violation, Kidane did not attempt to invoke the
affirmative defense because Hoversten was not TIPS trained. Id.
Hoversten was found not guilty of the charge and the citation against her was dismissed on May
22, 2007. State’s Exhibit 5. The administrative hearing complaint filed by the DPS followed on
November 8, 2007. Proposed Decision, page 6.
The Licensee does not dispute that the Licensee’s employees sold alcoholic beverages to persons
under age 21 during undercover compliance checks on March 3, 2006 and February 2, 2007. Nor does
the Licensee contend that the violation of February 2, 2007, qualifies for the affirmative defense. Rather,
the Licensee asserts that the Licensee is entitled to apply the affirmative defense to the first violation
because the Licensee’s employee had a valid TIPS certification card on March 3, 2006. Proposed
Decision, page 7.
The Licensee further asserts that if the affirmative defense is applied to the first violation, the second
violation would be a first violation making the appropriate administrative sanction a $500 civil
penalty rather than the $1,500 civil penalty and 30-day suspension imposed in the Proposed
Decision. Id.

The State argues that the Licensee is subject to the $500 civil penalty, even though the Licensee’s
employee was TIPS trained, because of the employee’s conviction under Iowa Code
§ 123.49(2)(h). Moreover, the State asserts that because Iowa Code § 123.50(3)(a) provides a mandatory
penalty, the Division has no authority to allow the affirmative defense provided under the pilot project.
The affirmative defense is available only when a licensee or employee is acquitted or found guilty under an
alternate code section. Thus, the sale-to-minor violation of February 2, 2007, is a second violation and the
administrative sanction of a $1,500 civil penalty and a 30-day license suspension is mandated by Iowa
Code § 123.50(3)(b). Proposed Decision, page 8.
The Licensee counters that the Division should be precluded from imposing an administrative
sanction for the violation of March 3, 2006, because the Division failed to inform licensees that in order to
claim the affirmative defense, the licensee had to ensure that the person who committed the violation was
not convicted under Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). Kidane contends that if the information had been
provided to him, he would have hired an attorney to represent Lindsey in the criminal case. Id.
V. ANALYSIS.
A. Program Eligibility
An issue indirectly raised is whether the Licensee satisfied all of the requirements to be eligible for
the affirmative defense offered through the Division sponsored TIPS training program. The record
reflects that Lindsey successfully completed the Division sponsored TIPS training on August 8, 2003, and
received a TIPS certificate valid for a three-year period.
The affirmative defense offered under the Division sponsored program was valid for two years from
completion of the program. Proposed Decision, page 4; Licensee Exhibit 1. The information distributed
by the Division to promote the program stated that licensed establishments participating in

the Division sponsored TIPS training program would be granted a one-time affirmative defense
valid for a “two-year period.”
The Administrator observes that the affirmative defense available to the Licensee for any underage
violations committed by Lindsey would have expired on August 7, 2005.3 The date of the underage
violation committed by Lindsey was March 2, 2006 – nearly 7 months beyond the last day the affirmative
defense was valid. The Administrator notes that, even if Lindsey had not been convicted under Iowa Code
§ 123.49(2)(h), the affirmative defense was no longer valid and would not have applied in the case.
While the answer to the first issue effectively resolves this appeal, the remaining issues will be
addressed to clarify the affirmative defense in future cases.
B. Effect of a Criminal Conviction.
The ALJ found that the preponderance of the evidence established that the Licensee violated Iowa
Code § 123.49(2)(h) a second time when Hoversten sold an alcoholic beverage to an underage informant
on February 2, 2007. The sale occurred under controlled circumstances with officers present. The
Licensee does not dispute that Hoversten made the prohibited sale on that date and offered no defense to
the violation.
At the hearing, the focus of the issue between the parties was whether the Licensee may successfully assert
the affirmative defense for the violation of March 3, 2006, when Lindsey was convicted under Iowa Code
§ 123.49(2)(h). The Administrator observes that the Iowa Legislature, through Iowa Code § 123.50(3),
has provided mandatory sanctions against a licensee’s license when the licensee or the employee or agent of
the licensee is convicted under Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). The Legislature has not provided any
3 The Division offered a second round to TIPS training, with the renewed affirmative defense commencing, on August 4, 2003,
and ending on August 15, 2003.

exceptions to the statute and the Division has not promulgated any rules providing an exception or an
affirmative defense to the statutory sanction. As such, the affirmative
defense is only an option when a licensee or a licensee’s employees or agents have not been
convicted under Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h).
C. Doctrine of Estoppel.
The Licensee also rgues that the Division should be estopped from imposing a sanction for the
violation because the Division’s public announcements failed to inform licensees that the affirmative
defense could not be applied when there was a conviction under Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). Id.
Essentially, Kidane argues that the Division should be estopped from imposing a $500 civil
penalty for the violation of March 3, 2006, because the press release and brochure announcing the
affirmative defense misled the Licensee. The doctrine of equitable estoppel is a common law doctrine
preventing one party who has made certain representations from taking unfair advantage of another when
the party making the representations changes its position to the prejudice of the party who relied upon the
representations. Ahrendsen v. Iowa Dep’t of Human Servs., 613 N.W.2d 674, 678 (Iowa 2000). The
elements of equitable estoppel are: (1) a false representation or concealment of material facts; (2) a lack of
knowledge of the true facts on the part of the actor; (3) the intention that it be acted upon; and (4)
reliance thereon by the party to whom made, to his prejudice and injury. ABD Disposal Systems, Inc. v.
Department of Natural Resources, 681 N.W.2d 596, 606 (Iowa 2004).
The general rule is that estoppel does not lie against a government agency absent extraordinary
circumstances. Bailiff v. Adams County Conference Bd., 650 N.W.2d 621, 627 (Iowa 2002). A person
seeking to invoke the doctrine of equitable estoppel against a government body “bears a heavy burden,

particularly when the government acts in a sovereign or governmental role rather than a proprietary role.”
Id. In addressing the application of the doctrine of equitable estoppel to government action, the Iowa
Supreme Court found that parties are charged with knowledge of the law and cannot ignore the plain
meaning of the law. Iowa Department of Transportation v. Nebraska-Iowa Supply Co., 272 N.W.2d 6, 14
(Iowa 1978).
The ALJ found that the Licensee did not carry the heavy burden of establishing that the Division
should be equitably estopped from imposing a $500 civil penalty for Lindsey’s sale-to-minor violation on
March 3, 2006. Moreover, the ALJ found, “While the Division’s written announcements of the pilot
project should have explained that the affirmative defense could not be asserted if the employee was
convicted under Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h), there was no showing that the omission of this information
from the press release or brochure was intentional and not just a mistake or an oversight. Iowa Code §
123.50(3)(a) is controlling and requires the imposition of the $500 civil penalty in this case.” Proposed
Decision, page 10.
Further, the ALJ found that by imposing the $500 civil penalty, “the Division Administrator is
clearly acting in his governmental role, in compliance with the statutory duties and obligations assigned to
him. The Division Administrator does not have the authority to waive or disregard the statute when
implementing the pilot project.” The $500 civil penalty imposed for the first violation of Iowa Code
§ 123.49(2)(h) is mandated by statute and must be imposed for the violation of March 3, 2006.
The ALJ further found that the Licensee violated Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) a second time on
February 2, 2007, when the Licensee’s employee sold an alcoholic beverage to an underage person. The

Licensee neither disputed the violation, nor offered a defense to the violation. The violation of February
2, 2007, triggers the mandatory sanctions provided under Iowa Code § 123.50(3)(b).

Le Boi (Licensee).
STATEMENT OF CASE
The Licensee filed a timely appeal of the proposed decision by an administrative law judge
(ALJ). That decision affirmed the Licensee was in violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h), based
upon a hearing complaint filed by the City of Des Moines (City). The basis for the ALJ decision
was that the preponderance of the evidence established the Licensee’s employees sold and served
an alcoholic beverage to an underage female confidential informant (CI #2) without exercising
reasonable care to ascertain whether she was under the legal age, in violation of Iowa Code §
123.49(2)(h).
In an Order dated June 27, 2013, the Administrator granted the Licensee’s request for review and
established a schedule for the parties to file objections or exceptions and present briefs in support
of their respective positions. The objections or exceptions and briefs of the appealing party were
due on or before Monday, July 29, 2013, and responsive briefs were due on or before
Wednesday, August 28, 2013. The Licensee and the City timely filed briefs.
On appeal, the Licensee argues that the ALJ decision is faulty because the Licensee was not
given full disclosure of the violation against them. Further, the Licensee asserts that there was
not sufficient evidence showing the Licensee failed to exercise reasonable care to ascertain
whether the informant was under the legal age.
FINDINGS OF FACT
The findings of fact in the proposed decision are adopted and incorporated into this ruling as if
set out in full.
1

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
The conclusions of law in the proposed decision are adopted and incorporated into this ruling as
if set out in full.
It is undisputed that the Licensee received the hearing complaint filed by the City of Des Moines,
which alleges a violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). The hearing complaint contains the
necessary elements as set forth in Iowa Code § 17A.12(2). Therefore, the Licensee’s claim of
not being given full disclosure of the violation against them is without merit.
Under Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) a licensee and the licensee’s agents or employees are restricted
from selling, giving, or otherwise supplying any alcoholic beverage, wine, or beer to any person,
knowing or failing to exercise reasonable care to ascertain whether a person is under legal age to
consume any alcoholic beverage, wine, or beer. The burden of proving compliance with the
statute is on the licensee. McCrea v. Iowa Department of Transportation, 336 N.W.2d 427 (Iowa
1983).
In the present case, the Licensee employed an age verification procedure in which a doorman
checked patrons’ identification, only allowing those of legal age to enter. It is undisputed that
the Licensee’s doorman viewed CI #2’s driver’s license which showed CI #2 to be under the
legal age. The doorman allowed CI #2 entry into the establishment after stamping CI #2’s hand.
CI #2 then proceeded to purchase beer from the Licensee’s bartender. The Licensee
acknowledges that the doorman misread CI #2’s driver’s license, noting that it was an honest
mistake.
The Licensee argues that they did exercise reasonable care prior to the sale of beer to CI #2,
since the bartender detected the stamp on CI #2’s hand and observed that CI #2 did not appear to
be under age. The Licensee’s age verification procedure relies solely on the doorman to verify
the legal age of its’ patrons before entry and is only effective if the doorman properly denies
entry of persons not of legal age. In the present case the bartender testified that he relied entirely
upon the doorman to verify CI #2’s age, adding that he conducted a visual observation of CI #2
prior to the sale. However, there was no further age verification process in place to ensure
alcoholic beverages would not be sold or served to a person under legal age. Ultimately, the
Licensee’s doorman failed to exercise reasonable care and as a direct result, the Licensee sold
beer to a person under the legal age.
Iowa Code §§ 123.50(3)(a) mandates a five hundred dollar ($500.00) civil penalty for a first
violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h).
ORDER
The proposed decision of the administrative law judge is supported by the record and hereby
affirmed.
2

IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED that liquor license number LC-37351, issued to DML 50315
LLC, d/b/a Le Boi, 508 Indianola Road, Des Moines, Iowa, pay a civil penalty of five hundred
dollars ($500.00) for a first violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). The civil penalty is due and
payable to the “Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division,” 1918 SE Hulsizer Road, Ankeny, Iowa
50021, on or before January 18, 2014. Failure to timely pay the civil penalty shall result in
further administrative proceedings.
The parties are hereby notified that pursuant to Iowa Code § 17A.19, this Order constitutes final
agency action for the purpose of Iowa Code chapters 17A and 123. This Order becomes final,
unless a party to the hearing files a Petition for Judicial Review with the Iowa District Court
within 30 days from the date of this Order.
Moreover, the parties are notified that pursuant to Iowa Code § 17A.19(5), the filing of a petition
for judicial review does not automatically stay execution or enforcement of the ABD’s action.
The ABD may grant a stay on appropriate terms or other temporary remedies during the
pendency of judicial review. If the ABD refuses to grant the stay or other temporary remedies,
the court may grant the relief.
