On March 5, 2013, the City of Des Moines (local authority) filed an administrative
hearing complaint against DML 50315 d/b/a Le Boi (licensee). The hearing
complaint alleged that the licensee violated Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h) when
the licensee’s employee sold beer to an underage person who was working as a
confidential informant for the Des Moines Police Department. A hearing was
held before Administrative Law Judge Margaret LaMarche on May 7, 2013 at
10:30 a.m. Assistant City Attorney Doug Philiph represented the local authority.
The licensee was represented by attorney Joseph Glazebrook.
THE RECORD
The record includes the Hearing Complaint, Notice of Hearing, the testimony of
Des Moines Police Officer Anthony Ballantini, Officer Ryan Doty, Jason Brooks,
and Jesse Wells. The record also includes City Exhibits 1-2, and Licensee Exhibits
A-D.
FINDINGS OF FACT
DML 50315 d/b/a Le Boi is a licensed liquor establishment (Liquor License LC-
38839) located at 508 Indianola Road in Des Moines, Iowa. (Hearing Complaint;
City Exhibit 1)
On July 21, 2012, the Des Moines Police Department conducted an alcohol
compliance check to determine whether liquor licensees would sell alcohol to an

DIA NO: 13ABD009
Page 2
underage person. Des Moines Police Officers Tony Ballantini and Ryan Doty are
assigned to the Vice/Narcotics unit and were assigned to assist with the
compliance check. Three underage females were approved to participate in the
compliance check with the officers. (Ballantini testimony)
Photographs were taken of all three underage females to show their appearance
on July 21, 2012 immediately prior to the compliance check. The officers
confirmed that the underage females were under the age of 21 by reviewing their
valid Iowa driver’s licenses. The officers searched the three females to ensure
that they carried only their valid Iowa driver’s licenses. (Ballantini, Doty
testimony; City Exhibit 2)
Underage female #2 has a date of birth of March 5, 1992. Her driver’s license had
the phrase “Under 21 until 3/5/2013” on a band next to her photograph. The
driver’s license was in a vertical format, which meant that she was under 21 at
the time that the license was issued to her. (Ballantini, Doty testimony; City
Exhibit 2)
Officers Ballantini and Doty drove the underage females to each licensed liquor
establishment. The officers accompanied the females into each establishment
and gave them money to attempt to purchase alcoholic beverages. (Ballantini,
Doty testimony)
The underage females arrived at Le Boi at approximately 10:20 p.m.1 on July 21,
2012. A doorperson, later identified as Jason Brooks, was checking identification
at the entrance to the bar. The doorperson asked everyone who entered the bar
for identification, regardless of their appearance. The doorperson refused to
admit two of the underage females after he reviewed their Iowa driver’s licenses.
These two females returned to the officers’ van. However, after reviewing the
driver’s license of underage female #2, the doorman allowed her to pay the cover
charge and enter the bar. At hearing, Jason Brooks testified that he apparently
misread the driver’s license. He testified that the writing on the driver’s license
was fairly small and he later found out that he needed glasses. Mr. Brooks
further testified that if he had seen female #2 on the street he would not be able
to tell if she was under 21 or over 21. (Ballantini, Doty, Brooks testimony)
1 The Case Investigation Report lists the time as 8:20 p.m. but this was a typographical error.
(Ballantini testimony; City Exhibit 1)

DIA NO: 13ABD009
Page 3
Officers Ballantini and Doty entered the bar after underage female #2 and
observed her go up to the bar and order a Bud Light beer from the bartender,
who was later identified as Jesse Wells. The bartender did not ask underage
female #2 for identification before selling and serving the beer to her. (Ballantini,
Doty testimony; City Exhibits 1, 2)
After underage female #2 brought the beer to Officers Ballantini and Doty, they
called a third officer to come to the bar and escort her out of the bar. Officer
Doty issued a citation to door person Jason Brooks for allowing an underage
person to enter the licensed premises after 9:00 p.m., in violation of the Des
Moines City Ordinance 10-09(c). Jason Brooks later pled guilty to the violation
and paid a fine. (Ballantini, Doty, Brooks testimony; Licensee Exhibit A)
The bartender, Jesse Wells, was issued a citation for selling alcohol to a person
under the legal age, in violation of Des Moines City Ordinance 10-06(9). This
citation was later dismissed by the city after the licensee prepared a written
training policy. (Ballantini, Doty, Wells testimony; Licensee Exhibits B, C)
Jesse Wells has been bartending since 2006. He has had Serve Save Advanced
Training and has had TIPS training on dealing with intoxicated patrons and false
identification. He had never been cited for selling alcohol to an underage person
prior to July 21, 2012. Mr. Wells explained that when a doorperson (bouncer) is
on duty at Le Boi, the bartenders rely on the doorperson to check identification
and stamp patrons’ hands. When a patron comes up to the bar to order a drink,
the bartender checks the patrons hand to be sure that it is stamped, which
indicates that their identification was checked by the doorperson to ensure they
were over 21. Mr. Wells recalled underage female #2 entering the bar with two
gentlemen and coming up to the bar to order a drink. Mr. Wells does not dispute
that the female was in fact 20 years old, although he believed she was over 21
based on the hand stamp. Mr. Wells noted that the underage female did not
appear nervous and looked like she could be over 21. (Wells testimony)
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h)(2011 Supp.) provides, in relevant part:
2. A person or club holding a liquor control license or retail
wine or beer permit under this chapter, and the person's or club's
agents or employees, shall not do any of the following:

DIA NO: 13ABD009
Page 4
...
h. Sell, give, or otherwise supply any alcoholic beverage, wine
or beer to any person, knowing or failing to exercise reasonable
care to ascertain whether the person is under legal age, or permit
any person, knowing or failing to exercise reasonable care to
ascertain whether the person is under legal age, to consume any
alcoholic beverage, wine, or beer.
(emphasis added). The Iowa Code defines "legal age" as twenty-one years of age
or more.2
A violation of Iowa Code chapter 123 by any employee, agent, or servant of a
licensee or permittee shall be deemed to be the act of the licensee or permittee
and shall subject the license to suspension or revocation. 3
The preponderance of the evidence established that on July 21, 2012, the
licensee’s employees violated Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h) when they sold an
alcoholic beverage to underage female #2 without exercising reasonable care to
ascertain if she was under legal age. The circumstances of this sale were
established by the credible testimony of two police officers who accompanied the
underage female into the licensed premises. As shown in City Exhibit 2, the
physical appearance of underage female #2 was consistent with that of a person
under the legal age.
The Iowa Supreme Court has recognized that, at a very minimum, the exercise of
reasonable care to ascertain the age of a person, as required by Iowa Code section
123.49(2)(h), requires a licensee’s employees to request identification from
patrons prior to selling alcohol to them unless their age is known or reasonably
beyond question.4 The Alcoholic Beverages Division has consistently held that
the reasonable care standard requires more than just requesting identification.
Licensees and their employees must carefully examine the customer’s photo
identification to verify that the person presenting the ID is in fact over the age of
21. A careless review of the identification is not reasonable care. 5
2 Iowa Code section 123.3(24)(2011 Supp., 2013).
3 185 IAC 4.8.
4 Jim O. Inc. v. City of Cedar Rapids, 587 N.W.2d 476, 478 (Iowa 1998).
5 See, e.g. Administrator’s Final Decision in D-2010-00244, p.3, issued 6/29/11 (“The ABD has
consistently held that the reasonable care standard requires more than just requesting the

DIA NO: 13ABD009
Page 5
The licensee’s employees violated Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h) when they
allowed the underage female to enter the bar and sold her an alcoholic beverage.
The licensee is liable for the actions of all of its employees. In an administrative
enforcement proceeding against the licensee for selling alcohol to an underage
person, it is irrelevant if the licensee divides the duties of checking identification
and serving alcohol between two different employees or if a single employee
both checks identification and serves alcohol. The licensee is still legally
responsible when alcohol is sold to an underage customer if the employee
responsible for checking the customer’s identification fails to do so or does so
carelessly.6
The driver’s license of underage female #2 was no more difficult to read than any
other driver’s license. Reasonable care requires that persons given the
responsibility for checking customer identification must have adequate eyesight
and light to do their job properly. If Mr. Brooks’ misread the driver’s license of
underage female #2, whether due to a mistake or poor eyesight, then he failed to
exercise reasonable care.
The fact that the criminal charges against the bartender were dismissed has no
bearing on this administrative enforcement action against the licensee. A
criminal conviction is not a prerequisite to suspension, revocation or imposition
of a civil penalty under chapter 123.7
Iowa Code section 123.50 provides, in relevant part:
123.50 Criminal and civil penalties.
...
3. If any licensee, wine permittee, beer permittee, or employee
of a licensee or permittee is convicted or found in violation of
section 123.49, subsection 2, paragraph "h", the administrator or
customer’s identification. A miscalculation or careless review of a driver’s license constitutes a
failure to exercise reasonable care.”)
6 See Motif, LTD, Bo-James v. Iowa Dep’t of Commerce-Alcoholic Beverages Division, 807 N.W.2d 158,
2011 WL 4378166 (Table in Westlaw, Unpublished Disposition, Iowa App., Sept. 21,
2011)(holding licensee liable for sale to underage person when bartender relied on doorperson to
check identification and doorperson did so carelessly).
7 Iowa Code section 123.39(1)(c)(2011).

DIA NO: 13ABD009
Page 6
local authority shall, in addition to criminal penalties fixed for
violations by this section, assess a civil penalty as follows:
a. A first violation shall subject the licensee or permittee to a
civil penalty in the amount of five hundred dollars. Failure to
pay the civil penalty as ordered under section 123.39 shall result in
automatic suspension of the license or permit for a period of
fourteen days.
(emphasis added). Pursuant to Iowa Code section 123.50(3)(a), the mandatory
administrative sanction for a first offense sale to an underage person is a $500
civil penalty.
ORDER
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED that for a first offense sale to an underage person
occurring on July 21, 2012, DML 50315 d/b/a Le Boi, Liquor License No. LC-
37351, shall pay a civil penalty of five hundred dollars ($500) to the Alcoholic
Beverages Division. The civil penalty shall be paid within thirty (30) days of the
issuance of this proposed decision.
Pursuant to the administrative rules of the division, any adversely affected party
may appeal a proposed decision to the Administrator of the Alcoholic Beverages
Division within thirty (30) days after issuance of the proposed decision. In
addition, the Administrator may initiate review of a proposed decision on the
Administrator's own motion at any time within thirty (30) days following the
issuance of a proposed decision. 185 IAC 10.27(1) and (2).
Requests for review shall be sent to the Administrator of the Alcoholic Beverages
Division, 1918 S.E. Hulsizer, Ankeny, IA 50021. Unless otherwise ordered, each
appealing party may file exceptions and briefs within thirty (30) days of the
notice of appeal or order for review. Within thirty (30) days thereafter, any
party may file a responsive brief. The Administrator may shorten or extend the
briefing period as appropriate. The Administrator may resolve the appeal on the
briefs or provide an opportunity for oral argument. 185 IAC 10.27(6). The
administrator may affirm, reverse or modify the proposed decision.
A party who is adversely affected by the proposed decision shall not be deemed
to have exhausted administrative remedies unless they file a request for review

Page 7
of the proposed decision within the time provided and the Administrator has

proposed decision.

STATEMENT OF CASE
The Licensees filed a timely appeal of the proposed decision by an administrative law judge
(ALJ). That decision affirmed the Licensees were in violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h).
The basis for the ALJ decision was that the preponderance of the evidence established that
employees of The Union Bar and T.C.B. failed to exercise reasonable care to ascertain whether
Melissa Vega was under the legal age when they failed to carefully review her Iowa Instruction
Permit that established her age as 19.
In an Order dated July 11, 2014, the Administrator granted the Licensees’ request for review and
established a schedule for the parties to file objections or exceptions and present briefs in support
of their respective positions. The objections or exceptions and briefs of the appealing party were
due on or before Monday, August 11, 2014, and responsive briefs were due on or before
Wednesday, September 10, 2014. The record reflects that all briefs were timely filed by the
parties.
On appeal, the Licensees argue that the ALJ proposed decision to uphold the violations of Iowa
Code § 123.49(2)(h) were not supported by substantial evidence. The Licensees maintain that
when the evidence presented at hearing is considered as a whole, it shows that employees of The
1

Union Bar and T.C.B. did take reasonable care to ascertain the age of Ms. Vega. The Licensees
further argue that the violations should be dismissed because the original ID was not retained and
presented as evidence at hearing.

The findings of fact in the ALJ proposed decision are adopted and incorporated into this ruling as

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

BASIS FOR DECISION
The Licensees claim that employees of The Union Bar and T.C.B. did exercise reasonable care to
ascertain the age of Ms. Vega when they carefully examined Ms. Vega’s instruction permit and
denied entry of “K” into their establishments. The burden of proving compliance with the statute
is on the licensee. McCrea v. Iowa Department of Transportation, 336 N.W.2d 427 (Iowa 1983).
Evidence presented at hearing shows that Mr. Garcia, the doorperson for The Union Bar, and Mr.
Smith, the doorperson for T.C.B., asked for and reviewed Ms. Vega’s instruction permit prior to
her entry into each establishment. According to testimony, Mr. Smith looked at the date of birth
and verified that Ms. Vega was the person pictured on the ID; while Mr. Garcia looked at the
date of birth, saw the state seal and reviewed the picture to confirm that Ms. Vega was the person
pictured on the ID. It appears that Mr. Garcia and Mr. Smith relied solely on the date of birth
printed on the instruction permit to calculate Ms. Vega’s age to determine if she was of legal age.
The Division has consistently held that the reasonable care standard requires more than just
requesting an ID. Licensees and their employees must thoroughly examine the purchaser’s ID to
verify that the person is the person pictured on the ID and that they are of legal age. However,
the actions of the Licensees doorpersons fell short of a careful examination of the ID. The ID
was vertical in orientation and titled “IOWA INSTRUCTION PERMIT", which should have
caused the Licensees to be more vigilant of Ms. Vega’s age. Moreover, just above the date of
birth is a red band with wording “UNDER 18 UNTIL 11/5/2011”. A careful review of the entire
ID for age verification would have shown that Ms. Vega was not of legal age.
The Licensees assert the violations be dismissed due to the original ID not being retained and
presented as evidence at hearing. However, Iowa Code § 17A.14 allows documentary evidence
to be received in the form of copies or excerpts, if the original is not readily available. The ALJ
thoroughly and accurately details the reasons for relying on the photocopy of the ID while
dismissing the Licensees assertions that the ID was not discernable.
The misfortune of misreading the date of birth does not excuse the responsibility of the
Licensees. A miscalculation or careless review of a driver’s license constitutes a failure to
2

exercise reasonable care. Motif, Ltd., d/b/a Bo-James v. Iowa Department of Commerce
Alcoholic Beverages Division No. 11-0328, 2011 WL 4378166 (Iowa App. 2011).
When Licensees challenge an administrative action and fail to produce supporting evidence to
satisfy the Licensees’ burden of proof, the decision should be affirmed. Gaskey v. Iowa
Department of Transportation, 537 N.W. 2d 695 (Iowa 1995). The preponderance of the
evidence demonstrates that the doorpersons did not exercise reasonable care to ascertain whether
Ms. Vega was of the legal age on November 16, 2012. As a direct result of the failure to
exercise reasonable care, the bartenders sold beer to Ms. Vega. Each employee’s failure to
exercise reasonable care is deemed to be the act of the Licensees and subjects the Licensees to
applicable penalties. Iowa Code § 123.50(3)(a) mandates a five hundred dollar ($500.00) civil
penalty for a first violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h).

Exhibits 5-7)
Christopher Smith recalled that the officers spoke to him after Melissa Vega was
served by bartender Adam Jarr. Mr. Smith asked to see Ms. Vega’s ID again, and
one of the officers showed it to him. Mr. Smith told the officers that the birthdate
looked like it said 1990. Mr. Smith testified that the officers looked at the ID with
their flashlights and agreed that it was difficult to read and did look like a “90”
but that it was a “93.” Mr. Smith testified that the line in the middle of the “3”
was completely faded. (Testimony of Christopher Smith)
Kurt LeClere was at T.C.B. on November 16, 2012 and was working in his office
in the basement when one of his employees came down to tell him that there had
been a problem with a compliance check. Mr. LeClere spoke to Officer Mercer
and asked him if he could see the ID used by Ms. Vega. According to Mr.
LeClere, Officer Mercer refused to show him the ID but told him that he should
fight it in court because “this ID is rotten.” Mr. LeClere understood that the ID
was “rotten” because it was hard to read. Mr. LeClere also spoke to Christopher
Smith, who told him that he read the “3” in the birthdate as a “0.” (Testimony of
Kurt LeClere)
Attorneys’ Professional Statements Regarding their Receipt and Printing of DPS
Exhibit 8 and Licensee Exhibits A, and B
When he offered Licensee Exhibits A and B into evidence, Attorney Joseph
Moreland made a professional statement concerning his receipt and printing of
the exhibits. Mr. Moreland stated that he received an electronic file from the
Iowa City Police Department. Mr. Moreland states that he produced Exhibit A
by printing the electronic file containing the photograph of Vega’s Instruction
Permit. Mr. Moreland stated that he printed the photograph exactly as it was
received by him, making no changes to its size or to the lighting. Mr. Moreland
further stated that he then reduced the size of the photograph so that it would be
approximately the size of a driver’s license, which is Exhibit B. (Professional
Statement of Attorney Joseph Moreland)

DIA NO: 13ABD029,030
Page 10
Assistant Attorney General John Lundquist provided his own professional
statement in response. Mr. Lundquist stated that he also received an electronic
file from the Iowa City Police Department that included the photograph of
Melissa Vega’s Iowa Instruction Permit. After redacting Ms. Vega’s license
number, Mr. Lundquist asked for the photograph to be printed on a quality color
printer. The result is DPS Exhibit 8. Mr. Lundquist had no further information
concerning the printing of DPS Exhibit 8. (Professional Statement of Assistant
Attorney General John Lundquist)
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
I. Statutory Prohibition of Sales to Underage Persons, the “Reasonable
Care to Ascertain” Standard, and Licensee’s Liability for Administrative
Sanctions Based on Employees’ Acts.
Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h)(2013) provides, in relevant part:
2. A person or club holding a liquor control license or retail
wine or beer permit under this chapter, and the person's or club's
agents or employees, shall not do any of the following:
...
h. Sell, give, or otherwise supply any alcoholic beverage, wine
or beer to any person, knowing or failing to exercise reasonable
care to ascertain whether the person is under legal age, or permit
any person, knowing or failing to exercise reasonable care to
ascertain whether the person is under legal age, to consume any
alcoholic beverage, wine, or beer.
The Iowa Code defines "legal age" as twenty-one years of age or more.4
A violation of Iowa Code chapter 123 by any employee, agent, or servant of a
licensee or permittee shall be deemed to be the act of the licensee or permittee
and shall subject the license to suspension or revocation.5
Iowa Code section 123.50 provides, in relevant part:
4 Iowa Code section 123.3(24)(2013).
5 185 IAC 4.8.

DIA NO: 13ABD029,030
Page 11
123.50 Criminal and civil penalties.
...
3. If any licensee, wine permittee, beer permittee, or employee
of a licensee or permittee is convicted or found in violation of
section 123.49, subsection 2, paragraph "h", the administrator or
local authority shall, in addition to criminal penalties fixed for
violations by this section, assess a civil penalty as follows:
a. A first violation shall subject the licensee or permittee to a
civil penalty in the amount of five hundred dollars. Failure to
pay the civil penalty as ordered under section 123.39 shall result in
automatic suspension of the license or permit for a period of
fourteen days.
(emphasis added).
A criminal conviction is not a prerequisite to suspension, revocation or
imposition of a civil penalty. 6 A license sanction may be based on a finding of
violation made following an administrative hearing.7
The Iowa Supreme Court has recognized that, at a very minimum, the exercise of
reasonable care to ascertain the age of a person, as required by Iowa Code section
123.49(2)(h), requires a licensee’s employees to request identification from
patrons prior to selling alcohol to them unless their age is known or reasonably
beyond question.8 The Alcoholic Beverages Division has consistently held that
the reasonable care standard requires more than just requesting identification.
Licensees and their employees must carefully examine the customer’s photo
identification to verify that the person presenting the ID is in fact over the age of
21. A careless review of the identification is not reasonable care. 9
6 Iowa Code section 123.39(1)(c)(2013).
7 Iowa Code section 123.50(3)(2013).
8 Jim O. Inc. v. City of Cedar Rapids, 587 N.W.2d 476, 478 (Iowa 1998).
9 See, e.g. Administrator’s Final Decision in D-2010-00244, p.3, issued 6/29/11 (“The ABD has
consistently held that the reasonable care standard requires more than just requesting the
customer’s identification. A miscalculation or careless review of a driver’s license constitutes a
failure to exercise reasonable care.”)

DIA NO: 13ABD029,030
Page 12
In an administrative enforcement proceeding against a licensee for selling
alcohol to an underage person, it is irrelevant if the licensee divides the duties of
checking identification and serving alcohol between two different employees or
if a single employee checks identification and serves alcohol. The licensee is
still responsible for administrative sanctions when alcohol is sold to an underage
customer if the employee responsible for checking the customer’s identification
fails to do so or does so carelessly.10
II. Analysis
The preponderance of the evidence in this record established that on November
16, 2012, the doorpersons employed by The Union Bar and T.C.B. (licensees)
refused entry to one underage female (K) participating in the compliance check
but allowed the second female, 19 year old Melissa Vega, to enter their licensed
establishments. In both cases, the doorperson asked Melissa Vega for
identification and examined the Iowa Instruction Permit that she presented
before allowing her to enter the bar. Bartenders employed by both licensees
then sold beer to Ms. Vega, and the sales were witnessed by undercover police
officers.
The sole issue is whether or not the two doorpersons exercised reasonable care to
ascertain whether Melissa Vega was under the legal age to purchase and
consume alcohol. It is undisputed that Ms. Vega’s birth date is 11/5/1993 and
that she was 19 years old at the time of the compliance check. Both doorpersons
looked at Ms. Vega’s photograph to make sure that the ID belonged to her and
both looked at her date of birth, which appeared in red just to the right of her
photograph. Both doorpersons testified that they read the last digit of Ms.
Vega’s birthdate on her Iowa Instruction Permit as a “0” and not as a “3.”
Moreover, both doorpersons claim that the last digit clearly appeared to be a “0”
and therefore they did not consider looking at the red banner above her
photograph, which stated “Under 18 until 11/5/2011.”
10 See Motif, LTD, Bo-James v. Iowa Dep’t of Commerce-Alcoholic Beverages Division, 807 N.W.2d 158,
2011 WL 4378166 (Table in Westlaw, Unpublished Disposition, Iowa App., Sept. 21,
2011)(holding licensee liable for sale to underage person when bartender relied on doorperson to
check identification and the doorperson did so carelessly, even though evidence supported the
finding that the licensee took care to train its employees, and the doorperson was generally
conscientious).

DIA NO: 13ABD029,030
Page 13
The preponderance of the evidence in the record supports the conclusion that
both doorpersons failed to exercise reasonable care when they examined Ms.
Vega’s Iowa Instruction Permit and concluded that she was over the legal age.
A reasonable person faced with these same circumstances would have subjected
Ms. Vega’s ID to careful scrutiny. The ID she presented was an Instruction
Permit with a vertical format. Although this does not mean that she was in fact
underage, both of these readily observable features on the ID should have alerted
the doorpersons that the ID required careful examination.
Both doorpersons looked only at the date of birth and the photograph on the ID.
Both claim that the last digit of the birthdate clearly appeared to them to be a “0.”
Given their claims, it is unfortunate that the original Instruction Permit is not
available for examination. Ms. Vega’s explanation about the timing of her
decision to get a driver’s license and the surrender of her Instruction Permit to
the Department of Transportation was entirely plausible and credible, however.
There is no basis in this record to conclude that there was any improper motive
behind Ms. Vega’s decision to surrender her Instruction Permit and obtain a
driver’s license.
It is typical for officers take a photograph or to make a copy of the ID used by the
underage person in a compliance check, and a photograph was taken of Ms.
Vega’s Instruction Permit in this case. It is also typical for photocopies or
photographs of IDs to be submitted as evidence in administrative sanction
hearings concerning compliance checks. A photocopy or a photograph of
anything may be less clear or crisp than the original. The quality of the copy
machine, cell phone, or camera and the care and skill of the person using the
equipment can all affect the quality of the resulting image. In addition, when a
digital photograph is printed, the quality of the resulting image can also be
affected by the quality of the printer that is used. It is highly unlikely, however,
that the quality of the printer or an adjustment of the printer’s lighting could add
any detail that was not present in the original photograph or in the original ID.
The record includes three printed copies of the photograph taken of Melissa
Vega’s instruction permit: DPS Exhibit 8 and Licensee Exhibits A and B. The
right side of the photographs in Exhibits A and B are substantially darker than
the right side of the photograph in DPS Exhibit 8. In all three exhibits, the last
digit of Ms. Vega’s birthdate is at least somewhat obscured because it is printed
over the dark collar of her coat. The last digit of the birthdate does not appear to
be a “0” in any of the three exhibits. The last digit is not legible at all in Exhibits

DIA NO: 13ABD029,030
Page 14
A and B. In DPS Exhibit 8, however, the last digit of Ms. Vega’s birthdate is
legible as a “3.” The center line on the three is not completely faded, as claimed
by Christopher Smith. The left side of the 3 is open and is not a complete circle,
as it would be if it was a “0.” These exhibits do not support the doorpersons’
claims that the “3” clearly appeared as a “0” on the original Instruction Permit.
In addition, many other establishments refused service to Ms. Vega, which was
also inconsistent with the claims made by Mr. Garcia and Mr. Smith that the “3”
clearly appeared to be a “0” on the original Instruction Permit.
If the last digit of Ms. Vega’s birthdate on her Instruction Permit was unclear or
difficult to read, a doorperson who was exercising reasonable care to determine
her age would look at the information on red band above her birthdate to verify
her age. Even in the poor quality copy submitted by the licensees (Exhibit A), the
writing on the red band is clearly legible as stating that Ms. Vega will be under
18 until 2011. The preponderance of the evidence established that employees of
The Union Bar and T.C.B. failed to exercise reasonable care to ascertain whether
Melissa Vega was under the legal age when they failed to carefully review her
Iowa Instruction Permit that established her age as 19. As a result, Ms. Vega
was served beer in both establishments, in violation of Iowa Code section
123.49(2)(h).
ORDER
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED, pursuant to Iowa Code sections 123.50(3)(a) and
123.39(4), that for a first offense sale to an underage person occurring on
November 16, 2012, Cream LLC, d/b/a The Union Bar, Liquor License No. LC-
33376, shall pay a civil penalty of five hundred dollars ($500) to the Alcoholic
Beverages Division. The civil penalty shall be paid within thirty (30) days of the
issuance of this proposed decision.
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED, pursuant to Iowa Code sections 123.50(3)(a) and
123.39(4), that for a first offense sale to an underage person occurring on

STATEMENT OF CASE
The Licensee filed a timely appeal of the proposed decision by an administrative law judge
(ALJ). That decision upheld the ABD denial of the Licensee’s liquor license. The basis for the
ALJ decision was that the preponderance of the evidence established the Licensee did not meet
the “good moral character” statutory requirement to hold a liquor license in Iowa.
In an Order dated February 27, 2014, the Administrator granted the Licensee’s request for review
and established a schedule for the parties to file objections or exceptions and present briefs in
support of their respective positions. The objections or exceptions and briefs of the appealing
party were due on or before Monday, March 31, 2014, and responsive briefs were due on or
before Wednesday, April 30, 2014. The record reflects that no briefs were filed by the parties.
On appeal, the Licensee argues not all owners were aware of the license denial or of the
telephone hearing concerning the appeal of the license denial. The Licensee asserts that after
being made aware of the nonpayment of unemployment taxes, payment was made, and further
maintains that the Licensee will file the biannual report paperwork after receiving the paperwork
from the Secretary of State.
FINDINGS OF FACT

set out in full.

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
The conclusions of law in the proposed decision are adopted and incorporated into this ruling as
if set out in full.
It is undisputed that the Licensee’s limited liability company has been administratively dissolved
by the Secretary of State’s Office. At hearing on January 6, 2014, through testimony of part
owner Andy Campbell, the Licensee claimed to have an issue filing a quarter of unemployment
insurance with Workforce Development, but testified that payment had been made and the
biannual paperwork had been completed and was ready to be submitted to the Iowa Secretary of
State’s Office, thus reinstating the corporation. Yet, in the appeal of the ALJ proposed decision
on February 26, 2014, part owner Jeff Krager alleges payment for unemployment taxes was
satisfied on Monday, February 24, 2014, and that the Licensee would file the biannual report
paperwork upon receiving the paperwork from the Secretary of State. Mr. Krager claims that not
all owners were aware of the license denial and subsequent hearing. This justification is not
persuasive.
The Licensee was urged at hearing to file the purported completed paperwork to reinstate the
corporation prior to the record being closed and the ALJ issuing a proposed decision. In the
Licensee’s appeal of the ALJ proposed decision the Licensee contradicts testimony provided at
hearing, claiming that payment was satisfied on Monday, February 24, 2014, and that the
biannual report paperwork would be filed upon receiving it from the Secretary of State.
The burden of proving compliance with the statute is on the license holder. McCrea v. Iowa
Department of Transportation, 336 N.W.2d 427 (Iowa 1983). The Licensee has failed to show
that their limited liability company is licensed to do business in Iowa. Therefore, the Licensee
does not meet the “good moral character” statutory requirement to hold a license in Iowa.

On August 15, 2013, the Alcoholic Beverages Division (division) sent a letter
denying the renewal application filed by DV2, LLC d/b/a Dam View (licensee)
for Liquor License No. LC-38112. The reason given for the denial was that the
licensee’s limited liability company had been administratively deleted by the
Iowa Secretary of State. The licensee filed a timely appeal and was granted
timely filed status. A telephone hearing was held before Administrative Law
Judge Margaret LaMarche on January 6, 2014. Assistant Attorney General John
Lundquist represented the division. The licensee appeared and was self-
represented by one of its owners, Andy Campbell.
THE RECORD
The record includes the Notice of Appeal; Acknowledgement of Appeal; Notice
of Hearing; Continuance Order; Proof of Service; and Division Exhibits 1-4 (See
Exhibit Index for description).
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. On or about August 15, 2013, DV2, LLC d/b/a Dam View (licensee) filed a
renewal application for Liquor License No. LC-38112 for the premises located at
410 E. 2nd Street in Davenport, Iowa. Andy Campbell is a 33.3% owner of DV2,
LLC. The other owners are Jeff Krager and Eric Englund. (Division Exhibit 1)

DIA No. 13ABD037
Page 2
2. The licensee’s limited liability company was administratively dissolved
on August 9, 2013 for failure to deliver its 2013 Biennial Report to the Iowa
Secretary of State, as required by Iowa Code section 489.209. (Division Exhibits
3, 4)
3. On August 15, 2013, the division sent the licensee a letter denying its
renewal application on the grounds that the limited liability company had been
administratively deleted by the Iowa Secretary of State. The licensee was urged
to take immediate action to reinstate its limited liability company before October
14, 2013. However, as of January 6, 2014, the Secretary of State had not reinstated
the licensee’s limited liability company, and it remained inactive. (Division Ex-
hibit 2; Testimony of Annie Adamovicz)
4. Andy Campbell spoke to the Iowa Secretary of State’s office in October
2013 and obtained the paper work that was necessary to reinstate the limited
liability company. Mr. Campbell discovered that his company had an issue with
a quarter of unemployment insurance that had not been filed, which had to be
rectified with Iowa Workforce Development in order to reinstate the limited
liability company. Mr. Campbell asked for and was given additional time to
accomplish this. As of the date of the hearing, this issue still had not been
resolved. (Testimony of Andy Campbell)
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
Iowa Code section 123.30(1)(a)(2013) provides that a liquor control license may
only be issued to a person who is of good moral character as defined by the
statute. Iowa Code section 123.3(34) provides the following relevant definitions
for “good moral character”:
26. "Person of good moral character" means any person who meets
all of the following requirements:
a. The person has such financial standing and good reputation as
will satisfy the administrator that the person will comply with this
chapter and all laws, ordinances, and regulations applicable to the
person's operations under this chapter...
...

DIA No. 13ABD037
Page 3
c. Notwithstanding paragraph "e", the applicant is a citizen of
the United States and a resident of this state, or licensed to do
business in this state in the case of a corporation...
The licensee’s limited liability company is subject to the same filing requirements
as a corporation. It is required to be registered with the Iowa Secretary of State,
to file articles of organization, to maintain a registered office and registered
agent, and to file biennial reports. See generally, Iowa Code chapter 489. The
licensee’s limited liability company was administratively dissolved by the Iowa
Secretary of State on August 14, 2013 and has not been reinstated. Unless the
licensee’s limited liability company is licensed to do business in this state
through the Iowa Secretary of State, it cannot meet the good moral character
requirements for holding a liquor license. Iowa Code sections 123.30(1)(a);
123.3(34)(c), (e) (2013). The preponderance of the evidence established that DV2,
LLC, d/b/a Dam View does not currently meet the statutory "good moral
character" requirement to hold a liquor license in Iowa. Therefore, the renewal
application must be denied.
DECISION AND ORDER
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED that the renewal application for Liquor License
No. LC-38112, filed by that DV2, LLC, d/b/a Dam View, is hereby DENIED.

NOW, on this 28th day of September 2022, this matter comes before the Administrator of
the Alcoholic Beverages Division (Division) on his own motion for a determination of the
threshold question of whether the cancellation of Espeulas Inc.’s (Licensee) liquor license moots
its appeal of the City of Ames’ (Local Authority) denial of the renewal of said license. See Riley
Drive Entertainment I, Inc. v. Reynolds, 970 N.W.2d 289, 296 (Iowa 2022) (declaring that
mootness is “a threshold question”); Homan v. Branstad, 864 N.W.2d 321, 327-28 (Iowa 2015)
(“It is our duty on our own motion to refrain from determining moot questions.”).
On August 10, 2021, the City of Ames denied the renewal of the Licensee’s liquor control
license. A timely appeal of the denial was filed by the Licensee and a hearing was held on October
13, 2021, before Administrative Law Judge Tricia A. Johnston. ALJ Johnston issued a Proposed
Decision on November 10, 2021, affirming the Local Authority’s denial of the renewal of the
Licensee’s liquor control license. On December 10, 2021, a timely Notice of Appeal was filed by
the Licensee with the Division Administrator.
The Administrator has recently learned that during the pendency of this appeal, the
Licensee lost control of the premises for which the liquor control license was issued. The
1

Licensee’s license was subsequently cancelled on August 12, 2022. In the interim, the Division
has received an application for a new liquor control license from a third party for the premises
previously licensed by the Licensee at 823 Wheeler St. Suite 5, Ames, Iowa. Through its license
application, the third party has provided proof to the Division that it now exercises exclusive
control over that premises.
For those reasons, the Administrator solicited the parties’ positions as to whether the
Licensee’s appeal should be dismissed as moot. Both parties submitted a response to the
Administrator on September 19, 2022 stating that they had no objection to this case being
dismissed as moot.
ORDER
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED that the Licensee’s appeal of the Local Authorities’
denial of the renewal of its liquor control license is hereby DISMISSED as moot.
The parties are hereby notified that pursuant to Iowa Code § 17A.19, this Order constitutes
final agency action for the purpose of Iowa Code chapters 17A and 123. This Order becomes final,
unless a party to the hearing files a Petition for Judicial Review with the Iowa District Court within
30 days from the date of this Order.

On August 10, 2021, the City of Ames (local authority) denied the liquor license
renewal application for Espuelas Inc. d/b/a La Fiesta Bar & Grill (licensee). The
reasons for the denial were listed on the form. (Exhibit A). The licensee filed a
timely appeal, and a hearing was held before Administrative Law Judge Tricia A.
Johnston on October 13, 2021 at 9:00 a.m. Ames City Attorney Jane Chang
represented the local authority. Ames City Clerk Diane Voss and Ames Police
Department Commander Jason Tuttle were called as witnesses and presented
testimony. The sole owner of Licensee, Luis Salazar, appeared with counsel,
Andrew Meyer, and presented testimony. At Appellant’s request, a Spanish
language interpreter was present as standby. Mr. Salazar did not utilize the
interpreter’s assistance at hearing.
THE RECORD
The record includes the Division’s Electronic License Renewal Application; the
Division’s August 27, 2021 Right To Appeal; Notice of Appeal; Acknowledgement
of Appeal; Notice of Hearing; testimony of City Clerk Diane Voss; testimony of
Commander Jason Tuttle, testimony of Luis Salazar, and the following exhibits:
Exhibit A: Letter dated 8/10/21 from Lieutenant Heath Ropp to Mayor
Haila and Ames City Council members regarding the liquor license
renewal for La Fiesta.
Exhibit B: Copy of citation and adjudication record from State v. Alberto
Amezcu Carillo, Story County Case No. STA0143906
Exhibit C: Copy of citation and adjudication record from State v. Alberto
Amezcu Carillo, Story County Case No. STA0144911
Exhibit D: Copy of ABD order dated 5/26/21, in Docket Number D-2021-
00077

ISSUE
Whether the local authority’s decision to deny Espuelas Inc. d/b/a La Fiesta Bar
& Grill’s renewal application for a liquor license for 2021-2022 was proper due to
evidence that Licensee repeatedly served alcoholic beverages to persons under
legal age.
FINDINGS OF FACT
Espuelas Inc., d/b/a La Fiesta Bar & Grill, holds a Class C Liquor License LC-
0045757 for the premises located in Ames, Iowa. Luis Salazar is the 100% owner.
The record does not reflect that Salazar has had any criminal convictions related
to his ownership of La Fiesta Bar & Grill. There was no evidence presented to
suggest the licensee is not now current in the payment of all taxes and utilities.
The evidence does not reflect that the liquor license has been suspended or
otherwise sanctioned for any liquor law violations. (Exh. A; Exh. B; Tuttle
testimony; Voss testimony; Salazar testimony).
The Licensee applied for renewal of its liquor license for a one-year license to
commence on August 19, 2021 and end on August 18, 2022. On August 10, 2021,
Ames Police Department Lieutenant Heath Ropp sent a letter to Ames Mayor
John Haila and Ames City Council Members, recommending that the liquor
license renewal for La Fiesta Bar & Grill not be renewed for the next year. The
letter informed the Mayor and City Council verbatim as follows:
A review of police records for the past 12 months found two liquor law
violations for the above business. During a compliance check on April 22,
2021 an employee sold alcohol to a minor and was cited accordingly. A
follow-up compliance check was completed on June 9th, 2021 and the
same employee sold alcohol to a minor again and was cited accordingly for
the second time.
So far, the Police Department has made recommendations to improve
their performance such as asking for customer identification and verifying
customer age, as well as utilizing the Iowa ABD Age to Purchase mobile
application to scan identifications to ensure validity.
At this time, the Police Department would not recommend a
renewal of La Fiesta Bar & Grill’s license for the next year.
However, the Police Department would be in favor of the
issuance of a 6-month license to give the business and the Police
Department a shorter period of time to evaluate changes to
ensure due diligence in keeping underage patrons from
obtaining alcohol. The process to initiate this would be for the City

DIA No. 22ABD0003
ABD Docket No: D-2021-00077
Page 3
Council to deny the requested 12-month license and adopt a motion
indicating the City Council would accept a six-month license application.
During this 6-month period, the Police Department will continue to
monitor the above location by conducting regular foot patrols, bar checks
and by educating the bar staff through trainings and quarterly meetings.
(Ex. A) (emphasis as in original).
The Licensee’s application was added to the City Council agenda for the meeting
which took place on August 24, 2021. Ames Police Commander Jason Tuttle was
present for that meeting as was the Licensee’s then manager, Amezcu Alberto
Carillo. The Council unanimously voted to deny the one-year license renewal for
the Licensee. Diane Voss testified on behalf of the local authority that the City
Council had previously denied a one-year license renewal for Patty’s Irish Pub on
March 9, 2021 for the same reason. That establishment came back and applied
for a six-month license which it received. Voss further testified that another
establishment’s one-year license renewal application was also denied on August
24, 2021 for the same reason. (Voss testimony; Tuttle testimony).
The Local Authority wrote “due to violations” as the basis for Licensee’s renewal
application denial. In its notes regarding the denial, it was noted that the “City
Council approved a 6 month license going forward. Applicant will need to apply
for new 6 month license.” (sic). (Application).
Appellant was notified by letter, dated August 27, 2021, of the denial of the
renewal application, however the six-month license eligibility was not noted in
that letter. The letter informed Licensee of its appeal rights. Licensee timely
appealed the Local Authority’s denial on August 30, 2021. As of the date of
hearing, Voss testified that the Licensee had not applied for a six-month license
renewal. (Right to Appeal letter; Request for Appeal; Voss testimony).
The Local Authority provided copies of the two citations and convictions at issue
regarding Amezcu Alberto Carrillo serving alcohol to a minor on April 22, 2021
and June 9, 2021. (Ex. B; Ex. C). On May 26, 2021, the Alcoholic Beverages
Division Ordered Licensee to pay a civil penalty of $500 as a penalty for violation
of Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h) for sale of alcohol to minors. (Ex. D).
Commander Tuttle testified regarding his recommendation and the council’s
denial of the Licensee’s renewal application. Tuttle stated when he spoke at the
city council meeting, he recommended to the council that the one-year license be
denied and the business be directed to apply for a six-month license, due to
having two violations for selling alcohol to a minor. Tuttle noted the same
employee, Amezcu Carrillo, made both sales. Tuttle stated he made this
recommendation in order to provide a shorter period during which they could
evaluate any progress the Licensee would make and would work with the
Licensee to make improvements. (Tuttle testimony).

ABD Docket No: D-2021-00077
Page 4
Tuttle explained that these citations arose out of compliance checks as part of the
program with the Alcoholic Beverages Division. If a licensee sells to a minor,
they have to do a second check to see if the licensee has come into compliance.
They started compliance checks on March 25, 2021 with all businesses. They did
the first check on Licensee on April 22, 2021. The second compliance check was
done on June 9, 2021 for Licensee. The last compliance check they did as part of
this program was on June 11, 2021. (Tuttle testimony).
Tuttle stated Carrillo attended the meeting and spoke with him afterward. Tuttle
explained to Carrillo how to apply again through the ABD and to have the owner
call him. Carrillo was at the time, the manager of Licensee. Tuttle was unaware
of any other violations by Licensee. (Tuttle testimony).
Tuttle explained at hearing that every time there is a violation, they review each
business. He knew of six businesses who failed checks both times and felt the
council needed to be consistent with these cases. There were two businesses on
August 24, 2021 that they voted on, and the other four would be voted on in the
future. Tuttle stated he made the same recommendation for each one; denial of
the one-year license renewal and advising the licensee to apply for a six-month
license. (Tuttle testimony).
Licensee, Luis Salazar, testified at hearing, stating he had applied for a six-month
license. He explained that Carrillo, the employee that sold to minors, had since
been fired. Salazar stated he had no other violations in the past two years. He
stated he has been working with the licensing division to keep complying. He
fired the manager, Carrillo, to make sure it wouldn’t happen again and has been
training employees regarding compliance. Salazar stated they have always done
training but now they do it more often and remind employees more often. He
further stated he shows employees videos and tells them they need to pay
attention, know the law, and check ID’s. Salazar stated they train on fake ID’s
and tell employees to make sure to ask for an ID and to look at the dates. He
stated that he tells employees to make sure they pay attention every time they
serve. He did a training the last week of January with another person from a
restaurant in Nebraska and attends meetings to do things better. (Salazar
testimony).
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
The Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Control Act (Iowa Code chapter 123) protects the
welfare, health, peace, morals and safety of the people of the state, and all its
provisions shall be liberally construed for the accomplishment of this purpose.1
The local authority asserts that the licensee’s license should not be renewed based
upon two violations of Iowa Code 123.49(2)(h) (2021), providing alcohol to a
1 Iowa Code section 123.1 (2019).

DIA No. 22ABD0003
ABD Docket No: D-2021-00077
Page 5
minor. The issue before the undersigned is not a revocation or suspension of the
license. The Local Authority denied the renewal of a license and therefore the
burden is on the licensee to establish compliance with the requirements for
holding a liquor license in the state of Iowa.2
As part of the application process, the applicant must provide a statement asserting
whether any of the business’ officers, directors, or persons owning or controlling ten
percent or more of the stock, or having a financial interest in the business, have ever
been convicted of any offense against the laws of the U.S. or any state or territory
thereof, or any political subdivision.3 At hearing, it was not disputed that Mr.
Salazar is the sole owner of the establishment and, as of this date, has not been
convicted of any offense.
As a general matter, a liquor control license may only be issued to a person who is
of “good moral character” as defined by Iowa Code chapter 123. 4 "Person of good
moral character" is defined, in part, to mean that the person has such financial
standing and “good reputation” as will satisfy the administrator that the person
will comply with this chapter and all laws, ordinances, and regulations applicable
to the person's operations under this chapter.5 A liquor license “shall not be issued
for premises which do not conform to all applicable laws, ordinances, resolutions,
and health and fire regulations.”6
A person holding a liquor control license and the person’s agents or employees
shall not sell give or otherwise supply any alcoholic beverage to any person
knowing or failing to exercise reasonable care to ascertain whether the person is
under legal age.7 Any person who violates this provision commits a simple
misdemeanor. If any liquor control licensee is convicted of a violation of this
section, the administrator or local authority shall, in addition to criminal
penalties fixed for violations by this section, assess a civil penalty. A first
violation shall result in a civil penalty in the amount of $500.00. A second
violation within two years shall result in a 30-day suspension and a civil penalty
in the amount of $1,500.00. A third violation within three years shall result in a
sixty-day suspension and a fourth violation shall result in revocation of the
permit. 8
As pertinent to this case, all applicants for liquor control licenses shall comply
with the following requirements, where applicable, prior to receiving a liquor

license, wine permit, or beer permit: cleanliness of premises; toilet facilities,
water, financial standing and reputation. The Iowa Administrative Code provides
that “[a] local authority or the administrator may consider an applicant’s
financial standing and good reputation in addition to the other requirements and
conditions for obtaining a liquor control license… and the local authority or the
administrator shall disapprove or deny an application for a liquor control
license… if the applicant fails to demonstrate that the applicant complies with
the lawful requirements and conditions for holding the license, permit or
certificate of compliance.”9
When evaluating an applicant’s “good reputation,” the local authority or
administrator “may consider such factors as, but not limited to, the following…
pattern or practice of sales of alcoholic beverages to 19- and 20-year old persons
for which the licensee or permittee, the licensee’s or permittee’s agents or
employees, have pled or have been found guilty, pattern and practice by the
licensee or permittee, or the licensee’s or permittee’s agents or employees, of
violating alcoholic beverages laws and regulations for which corrective action has
been taken since the previous license or permit was issued, licensee or permittee
misdemeanor convictions, the recency of the misdemeanor convictions.”10 In
determining the license applicant’s good moral character, the local authority may
review not only convictions, but other factors it deems appropriate.11
The following reason was given for denying Licensee’s liquor license application:
The Licensee twice served alcoholic beverages to persons under legal age. It is a
violation of Iowa Code section 123.49 for a licensee or a licensee’s agents or
employee to sell, give or otherwise supply any alcoholic beverage to any person,
knowing or failing to exercise reasonable care to ascertain whether the person is
under legal age.12 This does qualify as a violation of the alcoholic beverages laws
and regulations and calls into question Licensee’s good reputation in that the
licensee has not demonstrated that he will comply with this chapter and all laws,
ordinances, and regulations applicable to Licensee’s operations under this
chapter.13
The undersigned notes that the manager in question is no longer an employee of the
Licensee, having been fired for his repeated violation of this provision.
Furthermore, Mr. Salazar explained the measures he has taken to train his
employees and insure that this does not happen again. It was noted at hearing that
no further violations have occurred.

Licensee argues that allowing him to apply for a six-month license rather than a
one-year license is arbitrary. The Local Authority’s stated position that they would
approve a six-month license is not before the undersigned as it has not occurred.
What has occurred, and what has been appealed, is the local authority’s decision to
deny a one-year license.
As noted, the burden to show eligibility to hold a liquor license rests with the
licensee. Licensee’s employee committed two liquor law violations by serving
underage patrons, and Licensee’s employee pled guilty to those offenses. The
statutes and administrative regulations allow the undersigned to consider these
actions, if such actions demonstrate that the Licensee does not have the good
moral character required to hold a liquor license in the State of Iowa.
In evaluating the licensee’s good reputation, it is reasonable to consider the
pattern and practice of the liquor law violations by the licensee’s manager which
established that the licensee does not have such good reputation as will satisfy
the administrator that it will comply with all laws, statutes, and regulations
governing its operations. Based upon the clear violations of Iowa Code section
123.49(2)(h), the local authority did not abuse its discretion under the statute
and rules and was justified in concluding that the licensee has not demonstrated
that he will comply with this chapter and all laws, ordinances, and regulations
applicable to Licensee’s operations under this chapter.
DECISION AND ORDER
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED that the decision of the City of Ames to deny the
renewal application for Liquor License LC0045757 filed by Espuelas Incl, d/b/a
La Fiesta Bar & Grill, is hereby AFFIRMED.

proposed decision on the Administrator's own motion at any time within thirty
(30) days following the issuance of a proposed decision.
Requests for review shall be sent to the Administrator of the Alcoholic Beverages
Division, 1918 S.E. Hulsizer, Ankeny, IA 50021. Unless otherwise ordered, each
appealing party may file exceptions and briefs within thirty (30) days of the
notice of appeal or order for review. Within thirty (30) days thereafter, any party
may file a responsive brief. The Administrator may shorten or extend the
briefing period as appropriate. The Administrator may resolve the appeal on the
briefs or provide an opportunity for oral argument. 185 IAC 10.27(6). The
administrator may affirm, reverse or modify the proposed decision.

STATEMENT OF CASE
The Licensee filed a timely appeal of the proposed decision by an administrative law judge
(ALJ). The decision affirmed the denial of liquor license LC0028685 for the Licensee’s failure
to meet the standards of “good moral character” as required by Iowa Code § 123.3(34). The
basis cited by the ALJ was the Licensee’s corporation was not licensed to do business in Iowa
because it was administratively dissolved by the Iowa Secretary of State.
In an Order dated March 2, 2015, the Administrator granted the Licensee’s request for review
and established a schedule for the parties to file objections or exceptions and present briefs in
support of their respective positions. The objections or exceptions and briefs of the appealing
party were due on or before April 1, 2015, and responsive briefs were due on or before May 1,
2015. No briefs were filed by the parties on or before May 1, 2015.
Pursuant to 185 Iowa Administrative Code § 10.27(3), a notice of appeal of a proposed decision
must specify the following: the parties initiating the appeal; the proposed decision or order
appealed from; the specific findings or conclusions to which exception is taken and any other
exceptions to the decision or order; the relief sought; and the grounds for relief.
The Licensee’s notice of appeal failed to specify the specific findings or conclusions to which
exception was taken or any other exceptions to the decision, the relief sought, and the grounds
for relief. Therefore, a review of the record was conducted to determine whether the ALJ erred
as a matter of law or fact in affirming the denial of the License’s liquor license.

On August 21, 2014, the Alcoholic Beverages Division (division) sent a letter denying
the renewal application filed by Fish Inc., d/b/a Park Road Inn (licensee) for Liquor
License No. LC-28685. The reason given for the denial was that the licensee’s
corporation had been administratively deleted by the Iowa Secretary of State. The
licensee filed a timely appeal and was granted timely filed status. An in-person
hearing was held before Administrative Law Judge Margaret LaMarche on January 8,
2015. Assistant Attorney General John Lundquist represented the division. The licensee
was self-represented by its owner, Rick Brinkema.
THE RECORD
The record includes the Notice of Appeal; Acknowledgement of Appeal; Notice of
Hearing; Continuance Order; testimony of Annie Adamovicz and Rick Brinkema; and
Division Exhibits 1-4 (See Exhibit Index for description).
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. On or about April 9, 2014, Fish, Inc. d/b/a Park Road Inn (licensee) filed a
renewal application for Liquor License No. LC-28685 for the premises located at 306
Park Road in Waterloo, Iowa. Rick Brinkema signed the application as the 100% owner
of Fish, Inc., which is a privately held corporation. (Division Exhibit 1; Testimony of
Annie Adamovicz)

2. Upon receipt of the renewal application, division staff reviewed the Iowa
Secretary of State’s website to determine the corporation’s current status. The licensee’s
corporation was listed as inactive and had been administratively dissolved effective
August 8, 2014. The dissolution was based on the licensee’s failure to deliver its 2014
Biennial Report, as required by Iowa Code section 490.1622. (Division Exhibits 3, 4;
Testimony of Annie Adamovicz)
3. On August 21, 2014, the division sent the licensee a letter denying the renewal
application on the grounds that the corporation had been administratively deleted by
the Iowa Secretary of State. The licensee was urged to take immediate action to
reinstate its corporation, no later than October 20, 2014, in order to have its license
renewed. However, as of January 8, 2015, the Secretary of State still had not reinstated
the licensee’s corporation. (Division Exhibit 2, 3-2; Testimony of Annie Adamovicz)
4. Rick Brinkema has owned the Park Road Inn for 15 years and has 4 employees.
He describes his business as a small neighborhood bar. Mr. Brinkema admits that Fish,
Inc. has been administratively dissolved by the Secretary of State. Mr. Brinkema has
been unable to reinstate his corporation because the Department of Revenue claims that
he owes back sales taxes and Work Force Development claims that he owes
unemployment taxes.
Mr. Brinkema believes that he will able to resolve his issues with Work Force
Development when he files his back payroll reports with them. It is Mr. Brinkema’s
belief that he does not owe any money to Work Force Development. Mr. Brinkema
does his own payroll but has had difficulty filing the reports because he is not very
skilled using a computer and the reports must be filed with Work Force Development
electronically. As of the date of the hearing, Mr. Brinkema was planning to visit a Work
Force Development office to seek technical assistance to file the reports.
Mr. Brinkema concedes that he owes back sales taxes to the Department of Revenue.
He believes he may be receiving some proceeds from a life insurance policy that may be
sufficient to satisfy the Department of Revenue. It is unclear when Mr. Brinkema will
have these funds. (Testimony of Rick Brinkema)

CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
A liquor control license may only be issued to a person who is of good moral character
as defined by statute.1 Iowa Code section 123.3(34) provides the following relevant
definitions for “good moral character”:
34. "Person of good moral character" means any person who meets all of
the following requirements:
a. The person has such financial standing and good reputation as will
satisfy the administrator that the person will comply with this chapter and
all laws, ordinances, and regulations applicable to the person's operations
under this chapter...
...
c. Notwithstanding paragraph "e", the applicant is a citizen of the
United States and a resident of this state, or licensed to do business in
this state in the case of a corporation...
Unless the licensee’s corporation is licensed to do business in this state through the
Iowa Secretary of State, it cannot meet the good moral character requirements for
holding a liquor license. 2 The preponderance of the evidence established that the
licensee’s corporation was administratively dissolved by the Iowa Secretary of State
effective August 8, 2014 and has not yet been reinstated. The Division has given the
licensee ample opportunity to reinstate its corporation. The renewal application must
be denied because the licensee does not currently meet the statutory "good moral
character" requirements to hold a liquor license in Iowa.
DECISION AND ORDER
It is therefore ORDERED that the renewal application for Liquor License No. LC-28685,
filed by Fish, Inc. d/b/a Park Road Inn, is hereby DENIED.
